speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my presentation to the special committee on defence on June 27 last I stated that current procurement programs were being reassessed to determine if they would interfere with the exercise of future policy options. Included in the projects under review was the general purposes frigate program.
This project was approved early last year at an estimated cost of $264 million. This was only the cost of the ships themselves. A more detailed analysis of the cost of these eight ships, including support equipment for them, has resulted in a current estimate of $452 million. Even this figure would not likely be final, however, as some of the weapons systems proposed are still in the developmental stage. Certainly this means that some modifications would be inevitable.
While the cost of these ships has been a very important consideration, our review has taken into account other aspects. These ships were designed to provide in one type of ship an anti-submarine capability, an air defence capability for the fleet and the capacity to carry and land a limited number of troops and light equipment. Necessarily, in order to design all of these capabilities into one ship only modestly larger than the latest antisubmarine escort, it has been necessary to limit the capabilities in each field from those that could be achieved by more specialized ships.
As an anti-submarine ship the general purpose frigate would not be as effective as the latest R.C.N. anti-submarine escorts capable of operating and carrying the HSS-2 heavy helicopter. This helicopter can carry both a dunking sonar and a weapons delivery system. The general purpose frigate would carry a light helicopter which would have a weapons delivery capability only.
One of the central and most costly features of the general purpose frigate system is the provision of air protection for the fleet. This capability involves an estimated expenditure of $100 million for the missiles and associated equipment. The rate of technological change
in these missile systems is considerable, and the next few years may see improved systems available at less cost measured in relation to effectiveness.
The general purpose frigate would have only a small troop carrying capacity. If it should be decided that troop carrying capacity is a requirement of the Royal Canadian Navy, it could be provided by more economical and effective means.
The immediate effect of this program in respect of employment in the shipbuilding industry is not great, because the first keel was not scheduled to be laid down until December of next year.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, the government has decided not to proceed with the general purpose frigate program. I would hasten to add, Mr. Speaker, that this does not mean the end of our ship requirements for the Royal Canadian Navy. On the contrary, we are carrying out studies to determine both the roles and tasks which will be assigned to our navy in the future and the most economical way of implementing them. In the anti-submarine warfare field, for example, we are studying the relative effectiveness of all known systems, including aircraft, surface ships and submarines. Our review is concurrent with the NATO review authorized at the ministerial meeting held in Ottawa in May.
In the meantime, we are aware of the necessity of keeping alive the skills which have been developed in our shipbuilding industry. We are considering accelerating the major reconversion program of the Resti-gouche class ships, after sea trials of operating heavy helicopters from the Assiniboine, one of the St. Laurent class, have been satisfactorily completed this winter. In addition my colleague the Minister of Transport has an announcement of importance to the shipbuilding industry.
On our part, we will complete our long range plans as quickly as possible in order that the placing of orders for future requirements will not be subject to undue delay, and in order that the Royal Canadian Navy will have the best equipment we can provide to carry out its tasks effectively.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened with interest to the statement of the Minister of National Defence, and we are very pleased

Cancellation of Frigate Program that he has made the statement in the house instead of letting it out through other channels, as has happened during the last several weeks.
We are rather disappointed that this very important matter could not have been discussed by the minister with the committee on defence which was set up for the purpose of considering policy, although the minister did say that we could discuss and talk about policy after he had decided it. With that committee sitting twice on Tuesday and twice on Thursday, it is astonishing that the minister could not have appeared before that committee today and given us this information. Perhaps he will appear this afternoon and give an explanation to the committee.
What the minister has decided and announced constitutes a crippling setback to the navy program. I do not know what effect this is likely to have on the Canadian navy and on its morale. Certainly the impact on the shipbuilding industry of this country will be very severe indeed, because plans had been made for the construction of frigates and the whole question of maintaining the shipbuilding industry is just as vital as providing the ships; it is part of the war effort which a nation has to put forward if it is to be effective.
I wonder what the minister will have to say now in this connection, on the cancellation of this tremendous program, when he recalls to his mind some of the things he said in this house when the aircraft program was altered a few years ago in connection with the Arrow. The hon. gentleman was at great pains to express himself then at considerable length. The committee on defence has now got the truth before it from the former chairman of the chiefs of staff committee.
We shall have to examine in detail the lengthy statement which the minister has made, but I think we can only express regret than an immediate alternative for the Royal Canadian Navy has not been presented today.

I do
not intend to make any comment on the wisdom or lack of wisdom attaching to the particular decision which has been announced, but I should like to join with the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre in protesting against the way in which this announcement has been made.
The defence committee has been sitting. Ministers have appeared before it. This very matter was under discussion. Yet the Minister of Defence completely ignores the existence of the committee in his announcement today. It seems to me that if the minister


had said something about this decision to the committee he would at least have been extending some courtesy to its members.
It seems to me that the hon. gentleman's approach is part of the wrong way of doing these things. What has happened, apparently is that a piecemeal decision has been made with respect to one aspect of Canada's defence policy. It seems to me announcements of this sort ought not to be made until the over-all scene had been reviewed-and I understood the defence committee was set up to carry out such a review-so that we might determine whether or not a particular program would fit in with over-all strategy. The advantage of this approach would be that alternative programs could be discussed.
We believe greater consideration should have been given to the over-all effects of an announcement such as this. We should have been told what the government had in mind to take the place of the former program and what arrangements, if any, were being made to reabsorb the workers who are likely to be turned out of work as a result of the dropping of this program.

We
also are perturbed by a number of factors relating to the announcement which has just been made by the Minister of National Defence. One very important point to which reference has been made is the relationship of the defence committee to the whole program of national defence and defence policy. During the past weeks there have been a number of occasions when announcements have been made or reports have been circulated as to changes in defence policy and plans having regard to matters that have been discussed in the committee and about which we received no answer there. Yet we find that in a few days or a short time later public announcements are made regarding these issues.
Along with other members I protest against the way in which this whole matter has been handled by the Minister of National Defence. It seems to me that the committee is being pushed aside and pushed around. It is given some very minor issues to consider, and decisions are made on major issues before the committee can bring in its recommendations.
We have had the assurance this afternoon that the employment factor is being given very serious consideration. I would urge that no interruption in employment be permitted if this change is effected. We recognize that there will be reviews of all these programs from time to time, but we must see to it that the labours and skills of those who are engaged in these programs are used to the maximum advantage not only of themselves but of Canada as a whole.

I believe reference was made to an announcement to be made by the Minister of Transport perhaps tying in with this matter, and we will be interested to hear what he has to say in this respect.

Mr. Speaker, from the statement made by the Minister of National Defence, it appears that decisions are made by the department, by the minister himself, without the knowledge of the national defence committee. That committee is made up of members representing the various parties sitting in the house. If the minister ignores the national defence committee, what could justify the setting up of that committee?
The purpose of that committee is to inform the minister and help him make decisions. The minister should not come here with statements and decisions arrived at without the knowledge of that parliamentary committee which should have its say in those decisions. And particularly, a department as important as the national defence department, which has to make decisions once in a while for the whole of the country, should not act that way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a
statement regarding the shipbuilding program of the Department of Transport over the next few years. The department has completed its review of vessel requirements during this period and is proceeding with the implementation of a program for new ship construction which will cost close to $110 million

Statement on Shipbuilding Program and which will involve the letting of a series of new ship contracts during the years 1963, 1964 and 1965.
Planned new contracts during 1963 are as follows: New weather ship for the Canadian coastguard Pacific ocean station, contract already awarded to Burrards of Vancouver, estimated cost $9 million to $10 million; second new weather ship for the Pacific ocean station, tender call autumn of 1963, estimated cost between $9 million and $10 million; new automobile-truck ferry to operate between Nova Scotia and the east coast of Newfoundland, expected tender call autumn of 1963, estimated cost approximately $14 million; new triple screw icebreaker for the Canadian coastguard for use in Arctic, Atlantic and gulf waters, estimated tender call late 1963, estimated cost $18 million.
Proposed new ship construction contracts for 1964 will be as follows:
New ferry for the Borden-Tormentine service to Prince Edward Island; the estimated tender call is early summer of 1964 and the estimated cost $14 million; new ferry vessel for service between Sydney and Port aux Basques, presently in the planning stage, for which cost estimates are not final but possibly will be between $5 million and $10 million; the estimated tender call is late 1964; four additional vessels for the Canadian coastguard service to replace the old vessels Saurel and Chesterfield, and provide in addition certain smaller tender vessels for use at marine agencies. The new vessels would include two new supply and buoy vessels having icebreaking capacity for eastern Canadian waters, at a total cost of $13 million to $14 million, and two smaller tender vessels, one for the lakehead and one for Saint John, New Brunswick, at a total cost of between one and a half and two million dollars.
It is also expected that a further series of seven marine agency vessels, required by the Canadian coastguard, would be put out to contract in 1965. These vessels, which would be somewhat smaller in size, would involve an expenditure of between $10 million and $15 million.

However, before making my motion, I should like to state my reasons for doing so and say a few words about the present financial situation of farmers in eastern Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I was coming to my motion. Mr. Speaker, here is my motion:
Seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), I move the adjournment of the house, in accordance with standing order 26, to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, that is the necessity for the house to take immediately the necessary steps to help the farmers in eastern Canada before the St. Lawrence seaway is closed to navigation by the ice, which will make it impossible for western feed grain to reach the eastern provinces at a price that would give the farmers advantages they are entitled to.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the house- [Text]

Are there any other members who wish to offer suggestions to the Chair before I rule on whether this motion is in order?
The motion asks for leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purposes of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, and according to the various authorities often cited in this house since the 30th of September 1963, urgency means urgency of debate, and opportunity of course means the opportunity to debate the subject under discussion.
I rely in particular on a decision of Mr. Speaker Michener given on June 27, 1961, which will be found at page 7105 of Hansard for that date, when he said in part:
I accept the proposition that this is an urgent and public important matter to which the Leader of the Opposition draws attention. It is a definite matter of public importance. However, that is not the criterion in determining whether standing order 26 should be applied. The criterion is whether there is an opportunity to debate this matter in an effective way.

Now it seems to me that both on Monday and Tuesday of this week we had a supply motion, and I am informed that again on Monday and Tuesday of next week we will have a supply motion. This matter, although very important and having elements of urgency, nevertheless has-if I may use the expression-been under way for some considerable time, and the member could perhaps have raised it last Monday or Tuesday. I presume the hon. member will also have the opportunity of raising this matter next Monday or Tuesday.
It might perhaps be of interest to the house where I refer to citation 100 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which gives the essential element or reason for standing order 26 as we know it here. In citation 100 (8), although it refers to the United Kingdom, the principle is the same. It states:
Standing order 10 of the United Kingdom house, in force since 1882, also provides that a member may propose the adjournment of the house "for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent public importance". On the 13th of April, 1894 a member asked leave to make that motion to discuss "the neglect of the government to take measures for the relief of agricultural depression during the present session". As forty members rose in support of the motion, debate was allowed, but on its conclusion, the Speaker said: "I do not think that, under the standing order of 1882, a motion on a subject of this kind, having such a very wide scope, was ever contemplated. What I think was contemplated, was an occurrence of some sudden emergency either in home or in foreign affairs. But I do not think it was contemplated-if the house would allow me to state my views-that a question of very wide scope, which would demand legislation to deal with it in any effective manner, should be the subject of discussion on a motion for the adjournment of the house, because, if that was so, we might have repeated motions made by the opposition of the day, not so much in the direction of censuring the government for action which had been taken or not taken, for bringing to notice some grievance demanding instant remedy, as in the direction of wishing to introduce legislation on some particular subject. That is not the purpose of the standing order of 1882, and would, I think, cut at the root of the order".
In view of these authorities and what I have just said, I regret that in my opinion I cannot accept the motion.

Because of the fact that Your Honour mentioned that the matter could be raised on Monday or Tuesday, in view of that reservation I will not appeal the ruling of the Chair but will wait until Monday or Tuesday to discuss it further.

The house resumed from Wednesday, October 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon for second reading of Bill No. C-95, to amend the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, the other day we had a statement by the Minister of Finance on the introduction of the income tax bill for second reading. I might say, sir, that it had been my expectation the bill would rather closely follow the resolution which had been introduced. There were certain things indicated in the resolution to which I will refer later, particularly certain allowances for depreciation in distressed areas, and I refer to the figure of 95 per cent ownership in the plant as well as certain other things, which were not included in the bill. One must say that what appears in the bill is certainly a lot more restrictive than what appeared in the resolution or what was said during discussion of the resolution. However, I shall discuss that in greater detail later.

I do not intend to refer to any particular clause, Mr. Speaker, but I noticed clause 7, which I would have thought by now the minister might have included in any resolution because it has acquired a certain quality of semi-permanence. This has to do with certain allowances in lieu of family allowances, that are made to immigrants entering the country, and these allowances are then in the same category as family allowances for the purpose of income tax. This practice has been in vogue, I think, for about eight years. I am wondering whether it would not have been deemed that this is a regular feature of the Income Tax Act. Should we have been told quite frankly that this is going to be limited, or are we going to be faced with the re-enactment of this provision from year to year? I recognize that this is a carrying forward of something that existed in previous years, and it comes under yearly review.
I gather that the main burden of the minister's speech was that Canada faces a very serious problem of deficits on international payments. It was the view of the government -and this was nothing new, because he indicated it had been the view of previous administrations-that the best means of tackling this problem was in Canada selling more abroad. He said that the scope for increased sales seemed to be primarily in the United States; in actual fact I believe he used the term "the North American continent". If that was the objective, I wonder why greater emphasis was not placed on the providing of incentives for increased sales. In fact the one incentive that appeared in the Income Tax Act which was introduced a year or two ago is now being removed. I would like to hear from the minister why, after only a short experience, section 40(a) of the act is being repealed. Even if there has not been the expected advance as a result of this incentive, I think it has been in effect too short a time to show its full impact. In any event, Mr. Speaker, I think the minister should give us an answer in this regard when he makes his closing statement.
I rather think, though, that if the purpose of the changes in the act is to provide incentives, and in certain cases some disabilities, in order to change the nature of our balance of payments position, the bill now before us will do much less than was indicated at either the budget or resolution stages. First of all, we know that as a result of certain steps indicated at an earlier stage, investment in Canada received a rather serious shock, not only because of promised
Income Tax Act
action on this side of the border but because of action on the other side in the United States.
The minister was quite frank in telling us that at the present time it is virtually impossible to obtain money from the United States in any, shall we say, substantial quantities. There may be exceptions to this, but I know that businessmen who had plans for expansion or promotional opportunities in western Canada have said that at the present time these programs are absolutely dead because of the fear of action which may be taken in the United States. These programs of expansion and promotion are being put aside because of the uncertainty that exists with regard to the precise action that may be taken in the United States.
If it is the case that there is a drying up of money coming into this country, the minister's hopes of changing the nature of investment from equity into bonds will probably not come to realization. It will certainly not come to realization in the foreseeable future, because it will take some considerable time to restore a climate of confidence. Until this climate of confidence is restored there will not be the investment from the United States or other sources into the fields hoped for by the minister.
The other objective the minister hoped to achieve was the changing of the nature of investment from equities into bonds. There are certain incentives to try to change, shall we say, the nationality of investments. I am very disappointed in this bill, Mr. Speaker, because in spite of the difficulties that were pointed out at the resolution stage with regard to investment by Canadian residents, this problem has not been dealt with. Frankly, "Canadian resident" means nothing. What do we mean, when we say "resident in Canada"? Do we mean the 180 days usually envisaged in regard to the Income Tax Act, or do we mean the normal definition given to "resident" in everyday language, that a person makes his usual residence in a country? This is one point of uncertainty.
Again I come back to the point I made during the debate at the resolution stage, that "Canadian resident" means nothing in the context of capital inflow into this country. If the minister had the courage of his convictions in this regard, I think that as he was aiming for a 25 per cent Canadian ownership he should have said "Canadian citizen". I think he would then have been working toward the goal he desired; he would have been taking a step in the right direction. But he has not given any indication of even a first step in this regard in using the expression "Canadian resident" because there are scores

Income Tax Act
of situations in which this does not mean a thing. You have resident managers of subsidiary companies who are subject to recall, and who will hold shares in trust for the parent company abroad. This has been done in many cases. There are many ways in which shareholdings may be in the hands of Canadian residents but this may not mean anything, because behind the shareholding there is a trust agreement which provides that the shares are held on behalf of a foreign principal.
Therefore, in effect, if shareholdings are in the names of Canadian residents who are actually citizens of a foreign country and are here on posting by their foreign principals, I can assure the minister that the majority of them will be on the basis of trust agreements; the beneficial ownership will not lie with the Canadian resident. If the minister thinks that the Minister of National Revenue is going to go looking into all these things, the Minister of National Revenue will have to double his staff. The minister will really be creating an awesome task for his colleague.
I think it would have been better, and the minister would have received much more credit from financial critics and others in this field, if he had in this bill provided for that which he wished to achieve; that is, ownership in the hands of Canadian citizens. After all, 25 per cent means nothing in the majority of companies. In large public corporations it is a major minority holding which may give one effective control if the shareholdings are widely dispersed. But how many companies in this category would be affected by this type of legislation? I suggest to the minister that the majority of companies in this category would be private companies in the nature of subsidiaries-closely held private companies-in which a 25 per cent holding means nothing. There is no influence in a 25 per cent shareholding in companies of this kind.
I raise the point at this time, Mr. Speaker, because regretfully I do not believe the minister's objectives will be achieved with this this type of legislation.
We come now to the question of the withholding tax. I would like to know from the minister whether he has received advice from the law officers of the treasury board, or whether he has received assurances from the United States authorities that with the coming into force of this act with the provision- although it is to be effective only late in 1964 or in 1965-this will not be deemed to be an abrogation of the tax conventions between Canada and the United States. Further, if the effect of this is deemed to be an abrogation of the tax agreement, then does this mean that the full United States tax comes in at up to 30 per cent?

This is a problem on which the minister-should give us some information. He should tell us whether he has got these assurances; because if what I have said is to be, then with the stroke of an amendment, with some sort of a stick which is the counterpart of the carrot that he has provided with respect to this changing nationality of invested capital in Canada, he is wiping away a great benefit enjoyed by those people whom we have attracted with investment to Canada in the past. As I say, this is a very serious problem, and I hope the minister can give us the appropriate assurances. Otherwise he should withdraw his bill.
On the previous occasion I also spoke about associated companies, and I again regret that the minister has seen fit to bring forward this complete blanketing of related companies. While there has been abuse-and I agree there has been abuse in the sort of departmentalization of integrated businesses whereby it is sought to get the benefits of the so-called smaller companies at the lower tax rate-yet this is an essential feature of encouraging local capital and local management, particularly in western Canada. A man who has capital, and who is interested in investing it on an equity basis in developing businesses, will now be entirely discouraged because he cannot go to a small businessman who has got a good thing going but requires some capital, and invest 51 per cent in that business leaving the local man to manage and develop it.
I have seen this done in many instances, and I know of fine Canadian businesses developed in this way. Now, however, everything is going to be lumped together in the hands of the man who is providing the investment capital. The net result is that he is going to keep his capital at home uninvested. He is not going to use it in this way. Certainly he is not going to help the local individual to try to develop his business if the profits are going to be taxed at the 51 per cent rate, because it is not possible to differentiate between the share of profits of the local individual, the minority holder, and those of the majority holder. All profits go in at the same rate.
I suggest to the minister that this whole problem should be reviewed. I am not going into the question of the different tax rates. I am trying to remain within the principle of the bill, but I put it to the minister that I think a mistake is being made, and that in trying to plug certain loopholes he is shutting the door on much more.
This brings me to the further point, and I thank the minister for acceding to my suggestion, that an appeal from the discretion of

the minister with respect to associated companies and the dividend stripping provisions of the bill may now be made to the tax appeal board, though I say this with many great reservations because I do not think this appeal means anything. I would draw to the minister's attention the fact that the Canadian Bar Association also unanimously agreed it does not mean a thing. I am sure the minister has received a copy of the resolution adopted at this year's meeting of the Canadian Bar Association held in Banff, which incidentally I attended. I can tell him there was complete unanimity at that meeting in condemning the reintegration or reinsertion of the discretionary powers of the Minister of National Revenue within the Income Tax Act. The meeting felt that this was a retrograde step, and I can tell the minister there was no political partisanship in this because political supporters of the party to which he belongs were among the loudest in their complaints about it. There was no question of politics at all. It was a matter of principle by the lawyers of Canada that this was a bad feature and should be withdrawn.
After all, all the tax appeal board and the exchequer court can do in this regard is to examine that the minister has exercised his discretion in the manner prescribed by the act, that he has done nothing administratively wrong, but neither the appeal board nor the exchequer court will substitute their discretion for his. We know this as a matter of legal principle, so that the appeal provision is a complete nullity and I am sorry to see the reintroduction of ministerial discretion into the legislation. I know dividend stripping is a really difficult problem, but I wonder whether we are not here paying too high a price for the revenues which the minister deems he is losing through dividend stripping.
There are some comments I would like to make with respect to the increased depreciation incentives which the minister is providing for new industries in the areas designated under the Department of Industry Act. Here, Mr. Speaker, I must crave your momentary indulgence to refer to the fact that these words are used in the bill:
*-the capital cost of all machinery, equipment- and buildings situated in the designated area that were owned by the person-
I come to the question of what is meant by "owned". Is this owned outright? Has it been purchased on time? Is the beneficial ownership with the taxpayer? What is meant by this term "owned"? If I have bought machinery and equipment on a two year basis, simply paying 10 per cent down, do I own the machinery within the meaning of this term?
Income Tax Act
I may have bought it under a conditional sales agreement where ownership remains vested in the vendor until the purchase price has been paid. To all outward appearances I am the owner of that equipment, but in law I am not. The same may apply to buildings and property bought under an agreement for sale. I think we need an explanation in general

we can discuss it in greater detail when we go into committee-with regard to the proposed new section 71 A.
There are a number of other items, Mr. Speaker, which I should like to discuss, but this would be more appropriate at the next stage of the bill. Therefore I will conclude these observations on the principle of this bill by saying that I regret very much that the bill as put forward does not hold the promise indicated at the time of the budget. It is much more restrictive. I would say that the carrots and the incentives, in the tradition of ministers of finance, hold much less promise than do the sticks which may be waved.
I realize that the minister faces a very serious problem, but I think there are means still open to him to accomplish his objectives somewhat more effectively. As I indicated before, if he wishes to repatriate capital he should get it into the hands of Canadian citizens. If you have the courage of your convictions, then why not say so? If you are going to be hung for a sheep, as the minister certainly is at the present time, why come in as a lamb?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this legislation with regard to the Income Tax Act I should like to concentrate primarily on this very difficult problem of foreign ownership and control in this country. We need capital from outside, and we need it badly. We need foreign capital to assist us in our economic development and the attainment of a high rate of economic growth. On the other hand we certainly need a substantial measure of Canadian ownership and control in order to ensure our political survival.
So we have a very difficult problem to deal with, one which, on the one hand, advises us in economic terms that we should encourage the influx of capital from all possible sources outside the country, and on the other hand requires us to discriminate in some way in favour of Canadians, in favour of greater Canadian ownership, and in favour of individual participation by Canadians in the industrial future of the country.
Canada, Mr. Speaker, is a vast country, a country which has tremendous resources in respect to materials. But what it lacks is

Income Tax Act
capital, the mechanical means and the knowhow with which to put those great resources to work. One of the most substantial reasons for our high rate of economic growth and high level of income is the fact that we have had a great deal of assistance from outside in terms of low cost capital. A Canadian putting up money for industrial development today will ask for a return of something like 6 per cent interest on his investment. Foreign capital in recent years, including both foreign held bonds and equity participation, is asking something less than 3 per cent. This is cheap capital, and we need low cost capital in order to develop our country more rapidly.
But more important still, we have year by year been paying out interest on bonds; hence when the over-all return is 3 per cent to these foreigners, obviously the return on equity is down in the order of 1 per cent. The foreign investor in Canada's future has been taking out of this country less than 1 per cent return on his investment here. This is cheap capital. It is the cheapest possible capital Canada can get for the development of its resources, its industries, and for providing more jobs for Canadians. So there is in economic terms an overwhelming case for the encouragement of foreign captial in this country.
The result of this massive investment in Canada by way of low cost capital is impressive in statistical terms. Whereas roughly 40 per cent of Canadian industry was in foreign hands as far as ownership and control was concerned in the late 1940's, the proportion now is more like 60 per cent and it is steadily rising. Two thirds of the primary and manufacturing industries in this country are owned and controlled by non-residents. Roughly two thirds of all the workers in these industries are working for foreign owned and controlled concerns. No other country, at least in modern times, has had such a large proportion of its ownership held outside its domain.
Reference is sometimes made to the position of the United States prior to world war I. Then roughly 15 per cent of its annual income equivalent was owned by foreigners. In this country the proportion is more like 100 per cent. The parallel also breaks down in another respect; much of that foreign investment in the United States was in the form of bonds which would progressively and inevitably be repatriated. In Canada a large proportion of this investment is in equity and ownership and so resides, as long as Canadian law prevails and Canada continues to exist as a responsible nation in foreign hands.
Furthermore, the principal growth industries-oil, chemicals, electronics, and so on-

are in the hands of non-residents. These industries are growing at rates of 3 per cent, 4 per cent or 5 per cent a year. Only the industries in relative decline to the rest of the economy by and large are still in Canadian hands. This suggests that this proportion of foreign ownership will continue to rise. The big firms, the really large corporations which engage in industrial research, intensive market studies, and so on, are largely foreign. They are growing in size and the great majority are exclusively owned by non-residents. Only one out of four of the large corporations operating in this country sells any equity stock or ownership stock to Canadians.
I listened with considerable interest to the hon. member for Edmonton West, who criticized the 25 per cent ownership provision in the present bill. He said there was no guarantee that Canadians would end up owning much of this stock. Well, at least as a result of this provision there is an opportunity to participate in the equity ownership of large corporations which will take advantage of the tax incentive provided in the present budget.
What should we do in order to effectively repatriate at least part of the ownership of our industries? Repatriate them over the long run, slowly, measurably and in a straightforward, honest and predictable way. We might look to other countries. We might see the examples there. By and large the controls of other countries have taken direct forms. Legislation, for example, with regard to incorporation of firms requires that a sizeable percentage of the equity stock always resides in the hands of the residents of those countries, and legislation requiring that a large percentage of the directors be residents of those countries. The legislation frequently focuses on the resource industries, the basic processing industries and the utilities. These are the areas which are apparently of greatest concern to these other countries which have enacted legislation with respect to foreign ownership and control.
In most of the cantons of Switzerland no foreigner may own land. No foreigner may own registered equity stock. Obviously there is far more stringent legislation in Switzerland with respect to foreign ownership than there is here. France has always been concerned about the participation of non-French nationals in French industry, and in recent years France has endeavoured to convince her fellow members of the European common market, the OECD and so on, that legislation along these lines should be made uniform in all the western European countries with which France is affiliated. In Sweden, legislation provides that not more than one out of every three directors of a company can

be non-resident, and those who are nonresidents must receive the approval of the Swedish board of trade, which corresponds to our own Department of Trade and Commerce. In the United Kingdom, the bank of England scrutinizes each individual transaction with respect to take-over arrangements or alterations to the financial structure of corporations. Changes in ownership involving ownership passing from the United Kingdom to non-residents have not been frequent and before they are approved they have to pass severe tests in the light of the over-all interest of the United Kingdom, politically, economically, and otherwise. In Japan, no non-resident may own more than 50 per cent of the equity interest in industrial enterprise.
In the United States there are numerous examples of control. I will mention just one which is very much in the minds of some of those who operate tugboats, freighters and other vessels on both our coasts. No one who is not a national of the United States may own ships engaging in the coastal trade of the United States. Because of Canada's liberal legislation in this sphere, it follows that United States ship owners can operate up and down the coast of the United States, into Canada and up and down the coast of Canada. They can qualify for the 40 per cent subsidy with respect to shipbuilding and equip themselves with modern vessels with the assistance of the Canadian government; but no Canadian concern can carry on its operations both north and south across the 49th parallel. Thus this type of legislation favours United States ownership and control, and militates against the expansion of Canadian shipping on both our coasts and on the great lakes.
Also, Canadians have come off second best when they attempt to set up natural gas systems, electric power grids and works of a similar kind in the United States, due to the exclusive arrangements which exist below the border. They never receive a hearing; they have no chance of obtaining franchises. In this country, on the other hand, among the remaining utilities there is a sizeable participation by United States interests.
In respect to defence contracts in the United States, which engage much of the industrial capacity of that nation, foreigners are always on the outside track. This is another way in which foreign ownership of United States industry is kept within low limits.
I might mention some statistics which indicate the order of magnitude of Canadian investment in the United States. It is merely a fraction of 1 per cent of all the industry
Income Tax Act
there. It is true that the distilleries, the farm machinery concerns and some other enterprising companies do have substantial investments in the United States, but they are small in relation to the 60 or 70 per cent interest which United States corporations have in our industry here. Canadians have invested several billions of dollars in the United States, but United States firms have ten or 15 times as much invested in Canada.
We must obviously approach this awkward problem with moderation because we need access to this low cost capital. We must not bring in irresponsible measures, but we should at least be prepared to do something to provide an opportunity for Canadians to have greater participation in the ownership of industry in this country. I can think back to the time when my father was a young man in this country. The chance then was less than one in ten that he would work either for big government, that is, for a government department or a crown corporation, or for some big foreign owned corporation. In terms of expressing his own opinions the chances were better than nine out of ten that he would not be inhibited in saying anything he wanted to say. In my own generation the chance is one in three, or less, that a young man will be employed by big government or by a big foreign owned concern. When one works for government one must be circumspect with regard to the expression of political opinions. Large foreign owned corporations do not wish to interfere in the internal affairs of Canada and they definitely frown on their executives expressing opinions, matters of a controversial nature. If things continue to develop in the way they are developing, by the time my children are of age the chances will be 50-50 that they will not be able to speak as freely with respect to political and other matters in this country as I am, and as my father certainly was.
Let us consider the concepts of free enterprise on the one hand and of government initiative on the other. Canadians, in the face of the mounting degree of foreign ownership and control, will, I suggest, instinctively favour government enterprise because it will seem to them to be a Canadian communal effort, an effort having identity with themselves. I suggest they will tend instinctively to discriminate against free enterprise because they will inevitably come to think of it as being foreign dominated, something in which they have no vested interest, something from which they derive no obvious benefit. This hurts our Canadian image, in the sense that Canadians like to think of themselves, I believe, as prepared to take chances, to go out on their own and for opportunities' sake,

Income Tax Act
to forgo the security which usually follows from working in large government corporations, as civil servants, or for some large foreign enterprise.
There is need for some discrimination in our approach to this problem but there is also a need for legislation along the lines I have suggested. We need the capital, and so we must proceed in a thoroughly predictable way, a step at a time, with regard to this aggravating matter of foreign ownership and control. I should like to think that on this continent we continue to have a relatively free market with respect to capital-that goods and services can move freely, with the passage of time, between Canada and the United States; that people can continue to move freely and that money can move freely back and forth. We need this flexibility for our economic advantage but I think we would do well to remember what President Jefferson said many years ago.
His words had reference to King George III. He said:
You can never give to others the power to do something for you without also giving them the power to do something to you.
This is very important, and Canadians must remember this. We obviously have to weigh two great and desirable objectives. One is faster economic growth through capital assistance from outside, and the other is our independence as a meaningful political identity. I am sure we will manage it in a predictable, thoroughly responsible way and I would certainly urge the adoption of this legislation as one significant step down the road toward attaining these twin objectives.

Mr. Speaker, the whole purpose of this bill is to give corporations more scope and more tax concessions. I should like to deal today with only one aspect with regard to which I think Canadian corporations have already been given too great concessions and where in my opinion the departments responsible are not using enough care in examining what corporations are doing. I refer to the right of corporations to make contributions on a deductible basis to organizations which are of a non-profit or charitable nature.
It is not my intention or desire to interfere with contributions made by corporations or individuals to legitimate charitable and nonprofit organizations, but in my opinion this type of exemption is being abused widely. Two examples of what I consider to be real abuse came across my desk, and I presume across the desks of other members of parliament, in the last week or two. I should like to discuss these today.

One organization is known as the Equitable income tax foundation. As far as I can gather, the organization is made up mainly of people who are in the retail business. The president is Mr. David A. Gilbert of Toronto. The vice president is J. C. Munro of Winnipeg and the directors come from Prince Edward Island, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. I want to read a few sentences into the record from the letter dated October 11 which I am sure all hon. members received as I did. It reads in part as follows:
The Equitable Income tax foundation proposed today that co-operatives and credit unions should be placed on the same tax footing as ordinary investor owned companies. In a submission to the royal commission on taxation the foundation stated that co-operatives and credit unions, primarily because of their preferred tax treatment, are rapidly expanding their share of total business in Canada.
I want to bring this to the attention of the minister.
The foundation, a non-profit organization formed in 1962 to promote the principle of equity in taxation, stated that in the entire field of taxation in Canada it had found nothing to equal the discrimination existing under the present income tax law in favour of credit unions and co-operatives.
They also included a press release dated October 11 and I want to read a few paragraphs from it.
The Equitable income tax foundation proposed today that co-operatives and credit unions should be placed on the same tax footing as ordinary investor owned companies. In a submission to the royal commission on taxation the foundation said that co-operatives and credit unions, primarily because of a preferred tax position, are rapidly expanding their share of total business in Canada and have now reached a size and a level of efficiency that offers formidable competition to ordinary companies.
They also set out their recommendations to the royal commission as follows:
Taxation of co-operatives on net income before deduction of patronage dividends.
Abolition of the tax exemption of new co-operatives in their first three years.
Abolition of the tax exemption of credit unions and caisses populaires, and a requirement that they pay taxes on net profits before patronage dividends.
And tax treatment of patronage dividends in the hands of co-operative members on the same basis as dividends paid by corporations.
I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker. I do not question the right of the members of this organization to their views. I do not question their right to make submissions expressing their views to the royal commission on taxation, the government, the Minister of Finance or anybody else, but I disagree completely with their view on the desirability of taxing co-operatives as I believe the majority of the people of Canada do, and certainly as the majority of members of parliament do who

represent rural constituencies in which cooperatives have become so important as a way of helping rural people to make a living.
I believe this organization has a right to its opinions, but I certainly believe it is completely wrong that this organization, which has such partisan political views, should be able to receive contributions on a deductible basis. I think it is the height of arrogance for such an organization in such a fortunate position to be criticizing legitimate organizations like co-operatives.

speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question. Is the hon. member for Winnipeg North aware that contributions to the Equitable income tax foundation are not deductible as charitable donations under the Income Tax Act?

I can only go by the information I have. I have in front of me a pamphlet issued by the Canadian economic foundation and I can supply the hon. member with a copy of it if he wishes. On it I find these words: "Canadian economic foundation, a non-profit foundation, contributions are deductible".

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure of my ground here in dealing with something which is the subject matter of a question by the hon. member on the order paper and which is in the process of being answered. However, in answer to his question, whether the Equitable income tax foundation was given the right to receive contributions which are deductible for income tax purposes and, if so, on what basis was this granted, may I say that the answer, without reservation, is no.

If the minister would supply the answers to questions when he has them a member would not make a mistake. If I am wrong, then the information I have is incorrect. I put my question in good faith and I do not think I am in a different position from other members. I have questions which have stood on the order paper for close to three months without being answered, although not that one.
This question was put on the order paper on October 22.

I said, not that particular question. I put it on the order paper as soon as I had the information. We have had answers to questions on the order paper twice this week and that question was not answered. If I am wrong, I am sorry; but that is the information I was given.
The second organization, which I have already mentioned, is the Canadian economic foundation. Its head office is at 42 Charles
Income Tax Act
street east, Toronto 5. As I have already said, right on the pamphlet I have in front of me are the words: "A non-profit foundation; contributions are deductible". If that is incorrect, then the foundation is misrepresenting itself to the people from whom it is seeking contributions. The Canadian economic foundation seeks to undermine the labour movement and to thwart social progress with a Madison avenue type of propaganda imported from its United States affiliates, the American economic foundation and the American free enterprise productions, Morton Grove, Illinois.
The Canadian economic foundation is an operation which exists mainly to extract funds from reactionary and gullible employers who desire to fill the minds of workers in Canada with anti-social free enterprise propaganda. This organization has been used by two companies which have contracts with the United Steelworkers of America, namely Joy Manufacturing of Galt and the Toronto Iron Works. It has been used by the Dominion Rubber Company of Kitchener with very disastrous effects on the rubber workers union.
One of their pamphlets boasts that its techniques were used to settle a month old strike in three days. This included explaining the true economic facts of the situation in their plant. In another industry where employees were similarly informed, seven unions agreed to continue working under their old contracts for a period of 36 months without revisions or wage increases.
Now, none of the staff of the Canadian economic foundation are economists with professional training. They claim to be experts in communication, with simplified explanations of economic problems and simple solutions. For example, the Canadian economic foundation blames unemployement exclusively on high wages. It opposes social insurance such as pensions and health insurance that would take business away from private companies into government operated schemes.
This organization moved into Canada only within the last two years, and it is expanding very rapidly. It is now preparing to carry its economic study materials into all Canadian schools. It has already established a strong group in Saskatchewan to fight socialism. It would not be surprising if it were found to be preparing to play a big role there in the next general election. I do not object to that, Mr. Speaker. The government of Saskatchewan has fought the doctors, the insurance companies and many others. I do not object to any other organization, no matter what its name, going into Saskatchewan. However, I certainly object to this organization being classified by the government as a non-profit organization so that contributions to it are

Income Tax Act
tax deductible because this means that taxpayers, including people like myself, are being forced to subsidize this organization.
Would the hon. member repeat the precise name of the organization?

It is the Canadian economic foundation. I shall be glad to send to the minister this pamphlet and other pamphlets which are to be put out very shortly.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have only mentioned two examples. I wonder how many more examples there are in this country? I do not want to burden the department, but I am tempted to put a motion on the order paper requesting a list of all organizations in Canada that have been given this kind of exemption. Then, we could ascertain what is taking place. I know there are many worth-while, legitimate organizations which cannot get this exemption. There are citizens of Canada, trade unionists, making contributions to the organizational fund of the international confederation of free trade unions. This fund is used to develop democratic trade unions in the underdeveloped countries. Contributions to that kind of organization are not permitted as deductions from income tax. I think it is time the government had a very close look at this question of the organizations that are permitted this kind of special privilege, and ascertained how much money this is costing Canadian taxpayers.

Mr. Speaker, when he introduced Bill C-95, to amend the Income Tax Act, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) explained that the future of Canada was at stake in view of the state of economic inferiority in which we find ourselves at this time on account of our economic situation. He concluded his remarks with a warning which expressed both his fear concerning the foreign control of the Canadian economy and his hope that such a control would soon be removed so that Canadians would be masters in their own house.
On the other hand, as reported in La Presse for October 23, 1963, the Minister of Finance stated in Hamilton:
Canada must be more independent of foreign capital.
The minister added that we must learn not to depend on foreign capital.
Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit members are happy to see that the Minister of Finance is so well disposed and especially that he intends to take a step in the right direction. However, he is wrong to think that he will achieve his end merely by establishing a new fiscal policy.

The economic growth of our country is delayed by the heavy burden of taxes which must be lightened. Distinguished Canadians who are not in politics entirely agree with Social Credit on that point. For instance, according to Le Devoir, the president of the Canadian chamber of commerce Mr. Victor Oland, stated last October 8:
Proportionally to national income, per capita taxes have nearly doubled in a little less than 30 years. The strenuous efforts which are being made to remedy this economic malnutrition and which consist in giving transfusions of the patient's own blood, will end up in failure.
There, Mr. Speaker, you have a statement that our own Social Credit group is glad to support, and I do hope that the intentions of the Minister of Finance are along the lines of those of Mr. Oland.
Until now, the present Liberal government and its predecessors have acted as if they were expecting financial miracles to happen so that Canadians could become masters of their own economy.
I am amazed by the fact that politicians who are called upon to take over the destinies of our two nations can be so simple as to believe it is impossible for Canada to create the capital it needs to develop its natural resources.
Order. In keeping with the understanding reached last night by the different party leaders, may I suggest to the hon. member that he move that the debate be adjourned?
I so move, Mr. Speaker.

That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this house a copy of all correspondence, telegrams, communications and other documents received from the government of the United States of America, or any of its departments, or exchanged between the government of the United States of America and the government of Canada, or any of their respective departments, concerning the sale of wheat by Canada to the U.S.S.R., other communist countries and Japan, or pertaining to any representations made about the price of wheat sold to these countries.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is for the production of certain documents, correspondence and papers that have been exchanged or may have been exchanged between the government of the United States and the government of Canada or any of their departments concerning, specifically, the sale of wheat by Canada to the U.S.S.R., other

communist countries and Japan, or pertaining to any representations made about the price of wheat sold to these countries. I might point out to Your Honour that I consider the most important part of this motion to be the last section pertaining to any representations made about the price of wheat sold to these countries.
The basis of my motion is published reports appearing in the press to the effect that the United States has strongly protested fixed price sales. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from the Globe and Mail of October 10, 1963, carrying a dispatch from Washington. This article reads in part as follows:
The United States has lodged a strong official protest with Canada over the sale of wheat at fixed prices.
Department of agriculture spokesmen, who disclosed the protest yesterday, asserted that recent Canadian actions in the sale of wheat had jeopardized traditional Canadian-U.S. consultations and had undermined the world commercial market practices based on supply and demand.
Parliament is of course vested with the power of ordering to be laid before this house all documents that may be necessary in the view of its members for their information. Mr. Speaker a few days ago laid down a few guide posts concerning the production of documents. He quoted from May's sixteenth edition, from Bourinot and also from rulings made by Mr. Speaker Michener. One of those rulings was that the confidential nature of a document does not constitute a valid objection to its production. The other day when this motion was raised-I believe it was yesterday-the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) invoked the confidential nature of the documents and also stated that the filing of such documents would be a departure from normal practice and contrary to the public interest. With regard to the first point raised by the minister *-that is to say, the departure from normal procedure in regard to documents exchanged between two countries-I submit very respectfully, Mr. Speaker, that in this case there has been a very marked departure from normal practice in the fact that spokesmen for the United States department of agriculture have revealed, first of all, the fact of the protest and, second, have charged that Canada has fixed the price of wheat and has not complied with agreements made on that subject. By that action on the part of Washington, by their departure from normal practice by revealing to the press details that are normally confidential, I submit that it becomes, not contrary to the public interest but in the public interest that all these documents be tabled so that parliament and the people of Canada may have before them the full story.
Canadian Wheat Sales Abroad
The minister himself admitted that there has been a leakage, and certainly he does not take that very lightly. He has also denied that there has been any price fixing. That may very well be so. But at the same time we do have statements from the authorities in Washington to the effect that a protest has been lodged. We also have the statement to the effect that the Canadian government has given assurances to Washington that there will be no further departure from the agreements. We want to know, first of all, whether such a protest has been received, and if so, in what language was it couched? Third, has the Canadian government replied to that protest; and finally what assurances, if any, have been given by the minister and the government in regard to future sales of wheat by the Canadian wheat board
These, Mr. Speaker, are the motives which provoked my calling for the production of these papers. I think their production is completely within the power of parliament. There are precedents for the production of documents exchanged between Canada and other powers. I think possibly the latest precedent was created when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made a request last year for the production of correspondence concerning the drug thalidomide. At that time the government agreed to the motion, with the reservation that the permission or consent of the other power be first obtained. As a matter of fact, I think a good deal of correspondence was tabled as a result of the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to which the government agreed. Then again, because of the particular circumstances referred to above, it is certainly in the interests of this house to know about the details of the international wheat agreements and the agreements pertaining to the price of wheat. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit that this house should concur in the motion as made.
Before resuming my seat I wish to assure the minister that if he would agree to the motion, subject to reservations in regard to obtaining the permission of the United States government, its department of agriculture or any other department, as far as I am concerned that would be perfectly agreeable. There may be the question that no such documents exist. If these documents do not exist, I would like the minister to give a complete assurance in this regard. I would also like to be given specific assurances in respect to the protest which authorized spokesmen for the United States department of agriculture say was lodged and which they described as a strong protest.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this motion was made on October 23 I replied, as the hon. member who has just spoken said, that to table confidential information of the kind requested by him would be both a departure from normal usage in the intergovernmental exchange of confidential information and would not be in the public interest. For these reasons I respectfully requested him to withdraw his motion. Now, for the reasons he has stated today, he decided not to do so and the motion is down for debate.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that an important question of principle is involved here, and it is not a question that I would speak about in quite the same terms as my hon. friend. He cited instances in which these documents had been revealed by the government on request. I can imagine there are circumstances, and have been circumstances, in which it has been in the public interest for documents exchanged between governments to be presented here in the House of Commons, or otherwise revealed. My argument is that these exchanges on a subject such as the sale of wheat and the pricing policies of the respective governments are not the kind of documents that it would be in the public interest to reveal, because it would have an adverse effect upon the Canadian interest and upon the operations, in particular, of the Canadian wheat board.

May I ask a question at this point. Does the minister consider that there has been, or has not been, a departure from normal practice by the fact that spokesmen for the department of agriculture in the United States have made the statements they have made, to which I referred a few minutes ago?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that certain information which we regarded as confidential has been revealed, and I must take it from what appeared in the newspapers that this information was revealed by the United States department of agriculture. But I do not really think, and I am sure my hon. friend would not suggest, that for this reason we should on our part reveal information that it would not be in the interests of either country to reveal.
It may be that the United States officials thought it was in their interest. I do not think it was in their interest, and it certainly was not in ours; and I therefore do not intend to participate in the contest by revealing information that can only be embarrassing to both sides.
May I ask the minister a question. Will he now disclose to us the price that the Russians are paying for the wheat?

Mr. Speaker, I really think I ought to get on seriously with the question that has been raised by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue when he put forward his motion. Of course I do not intend to reveal these prices. I have made this a matter of principle.

The hon. gentleman has not identified the reports from Washington.
$1.74 a bushel.

No. I shall not confirm that price.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the reason that I do take very serious objection to this motion is that I really believe it would interfere in the future with the kind of consultations that I consider ought to be going on between our two governments and which have gone on in the past to our mutual benefit.
I can recall when these consultations were begun. It is many years ago now since I was an official and had the privilege of leading the Canadian team that went to Washington to initiate the discussions and consultations on wheat policy. During those years we had very useful consultations, and there were useful consultations more recently when the government of which my hon. friend was a member was in office. I know, from having looked at the files, that these consultations were very useful, and I do not really think it would be helpful to the continuation of these very useful consultations if I were to agree to this motion and were to table documents of the kind that he has requested.
For example, to illustrate the kind of consultations that have gone on, I said in answer to some questions in the House of Commons-and I think also in statements I made on motions-that during the negotiation of the very large contract with the Soviet union the Canadian government, on its own motion, let the United States government know about the negotiations because we believed that it was part of our responsibility to let the United States know that a massive transaction of international importance was under negotiation. Later, when the negotiations were concluded, and when it appeared that the Russians might go to the United States to buy wheat to meet their requirements, the United States government asked us if they could see the agreement and the other documents relating thereto.
That was a very useful consultation. I have looked at the files, after this motion was put on the order paper, to see what documents there were relating to that particular

transaction, and indeed there are no documents. All the documents on the flies are the documents I tabled in the House of Commons when I produced the copy of the Russian agreement and the copies of the various letters that were signed at the same time. There was nothing else.
These documents were handed by our ambassador, or one of his assistants, to members of the United States administration in Washington. I could have stated, if I had wished, to the hon. gentleman that I had been unable to discover documents of the kind referred to in this motion, but I did not want to do that because I believe in principle that documents of this kind which might exist, which I have been unable to discover, which may for example exist in the files of the Canadian embassy in Washington, should not be revealed. To produce such documents would inhibit the consultations that otherwise would have gone on.
Do I understand the minister can give no assurance that such documents do not exist?

That is right, and I do not intend to give any such assurance. 1 am talking about the nature of the consultations that must go on. Most of them are oral; sometimes they may be written; but whether oral or written, it is only going to inhibit that friendly exchange of information if this kind of motion should be approved by the House of Commons and these documents have to be produced.
I do not think even to ask the United States government whether they would be agreeable to having these documents published would be helpful. As 1 said when 1 made my original statement to table confidential information of the kind requested by the hon. member would be both a departure from normal usage in the intergovernmental exchange of confidential information and not in the public interest. For these reasons I submit that the house should not approve this motion and I respectfully urge the hon. gentleman, when I have finished my remarks, to withdraw his motion because I do not believe it is in the interests of Canada.
However, I should like to speak more particularly about one or two questions which the hon. member put to me during the course of his remarks. He asked me whether any assurances had been given to the United States government about the pricing policies of the Canadian wheat board. I should like to assure him that no such assurances were given at any time. There were consultations, as there have been many times in the past, about the respective wheat policies of the two governments; but at no time has the
Canadian Wheat Sales Abroad wheat board or any official or minister of the Canadian government given an assurance about Canadian wheat prices.
With this in mind, was any price given to the United States authorities as the bargaining price?

No. As far as I am aware we told the United States government exactly what I have told this house-in other words, that the Canadian wheat board sold wheat at the price posted on that day to whichever customers bought wheat on that day. That is the exact information given by the Canadian government and the Canadian wheat board to all who inquire. We do not reveal to anyone the prices at which the wheat board enters into transactions with its customers. It is very easy to look at the posted prices of the wheat board on any day a sale is made to find out the price at which a sale was made. Of course you would have to know what grade had been purchased, in what position, and so on; but if you wanted to know the wheat board prices on that day you need only look at the list.
May I ask a question of the minister. Does he mean he cannot give the price of wheat per bushel sold to U.S. buyers?

I know the price because the wheat board has told me; but I do not, because the wheat board does not, reveal that price to anybody. That is a matter of policy on the part of the Canadian wheat board. As I say, it does post prices every day at which it is prepared to sell the respective grades of wheat then on offer; but it does not reveal what has been purchased by any particular customer at any particular price.
Is there any reason for not revealing such a price?
Yes; because the Canadian wheat board believes it would not be in the interests of its customers, and because it wishes to retain the good will of its customers.

If you will permit another question, if a person wanted to compare prices of wheat for export with those on the internal market, how would he get the two
prices?

The wheat board publishes its daily prices every day and he has only to look at the posting. If he wishes to know what price the wheat board sells at today he will find it listed in the Winnipeg Free Press.

Would the minister care to comment on the charge made by the U.S.

Canadian Wheat Sales Abroad spokesman that the Canadian wheat board sold wheat to the Japanese at five cents a bushel below the prevailing price?

I should like to say a word about this. There seems to be some misunderstanding because of the use of the words "prevailing price". The only prevailing price for Canadian wheat is the price at which the Canadian wheat board offers it. When a remark is made that the sale to Japan was at five cents below the prevailing market price, that statement has no meaning. The fact of the matter is that the price at which the Japanese sale was made was approximately five cents higher-if you use No. 1 northern as the basis-than the price at which wheat was sold to the Soviet union. Since that time the price of No. 1 northern has risen another three cents according to the posted prices of the Canadian wheat board.
What about the long term contracts?

These transactions by the wheat board, as I have said on many occasions, are made at their offered, posted prices on the day on which the sale is made. Any statement that the sales to the Japanese were made below the market price is meaningless. There is only one market price as far as Canadian wheat is concerned, and that is the price at which the Canadian wheat board sells wheat.
Do the United States and Canada have, shall we say, a gentleman's agreement in that regard?

No, there is no agreement of that kind between Canada and the United States. There is only an agreement to consult. As I said when I was explaining the policy of the Canadian wheat board, which incidentally had the full approval of all spokesmen on the other side of this house who followed me on that occasion, the Canadian wheat board decided to protect its regular customers and in pursuance of that policy did enter into a sale to Japan for delivery over the next eight months at the price which prevailed on the day of the sale.
May I ask if in this particular case there was consultation with the United States?
I do not know what the hon. gentleman means by consultation. If he means was there agreement-
The minister himself said there was no agreement but that we do consult, so I want to know whether there was consultation, or did he consult?
At about the time the transaction was entered into there were consultations proceeding between the two governments.

I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I fully approve of the methods used by the Canadian wheat board for selling grain, but with these long term agreements is there not a clause whereby, at a certain time, say every six months or every three months, the price would be reviewed by the Canadian wheat board and the party to whom they sold the wheat? So far the method applied by the Canadian wheat board over the years meets with the approval of the farmers, except in cases of long term agreements, which perhaps should be reviewed from time to time on account of fluctuating prices on the world market. Would the minister answer that question?

The Canadian wheat board is prepared to enter into contracts for early delivery and for delivery over a period of time. It is not prepared to enter into contracts for delivery, for example, beyond the end of the current crop year. It has, however, entered into some contracts extending up to the end of the current crop year, the most notable being the sale to the Soviet union and that made to Japan. The Canadian wheat board has not been prepared to enter into any sales for delivery beyond that date. That is the policy of the Canadian wheat board at the present time, and they believe it appropriate to present circumstances. There are some sales which are for much earlier delivery to other countries; but in order to protect the position of its regular customers during this current crop year it entered into some transactions in which the price is fixed for delivery during the balance of this crop year.
Do I have to go to North Dakota to find out the price at which the wheat board sells wheat to Russia, or are you going to give it to us?

I think I have answered this question on a number of occasions. I would not do damage to the Canadian wheat board and I hope my hon. friend would not. I hope he agrees that it would not be in the interests of the marketing of Canadian wheat to reveal the prices at which the contracts are entered into.

board involved or did any of the grain exchanges contribute to this contract, either directly or indirectly?
The answer to that is that the Soviet government employed the private grain trade to act as its agent in its purchases from the Canadian wheat board.
Does that mean that some of the Canadian grain exchanges contributed to the making of this contract?

Do we know how much it costs the country for their services?
The costs were paid by the Soviet union. I have no idea what they paid.
