The devaluation of the Canadian dollar took place before we took office. My understanding of the policy of the Canadian wheat board is that it raised its price in Canadian dollars to the equivalent of what it had been before the dollar was devalued and stabilized, so it did have the result of increasing the return for the western farmers and, I believe, it did have the effect of contributing to the increase in sales.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to move the second reading of Bill No. S-36, an act respecting the Canadian Union Conference Corporation of Seventh-day Adventists. In the township of Darlington at the westerly extremity of my riding we are pleased to have many members of this church, and in the city of Oshawa, only a block or two west of the westerly limit of my riding, is located the administrative offices of the Seventh-day Adventist church in Canada as well as a large modern new church and a college.
The Seventh-day Adventists are known throughout the world for their missionary work not only in the spreading of the gospel but in the practice of medicine, the administration and construction of hospitals and general assistance to mankind, both spiritual and material, in all parts of the globe. The Seventh-day Adventist church is a Protestant Christian denomination. The movement had its beginning early in the 19th century and the church was officially organized in 1860. Today members of this church are found everywhere across our nation and there are over a million and a quarter members around the globe.
Hon. members will have studied the bill now before the house and I will not go into details with respect to its provisions. The bill amends the legislation enacted in 1955 which created the Canadian Union Conference Corporation of Seventh-day Adventists, which is the corporate entity representing the Seventh-day Adventist church in Canada. Clause 1 of the bill changes the somewhat cumbersome name of the Canadian Union Conference Corporation of Seventh-day Adventists to the shorter name of the Seventh-day Adventist Church in Canada or Eglise Adventiste du Septieme Jour au Canada.
Clause 2 removes the limitation on the powers of the corporation to hold land. Clause 3 enlarges and clarifies the powers of the corporation in connection with the printing

and distribution of works for religious education, art and science. Clause 4 of the bill makes it clear that the regular general meetings of the corporation need be held only once in every four years. Thus, the general meeting may then be held at the same time as the quadriennial general conference of the church.
Generally then, Mr. Speaker, this bill is designed to update the legislation, to bring it more into conformity with general corporate practice as well as with the current requirements of the corporation, if it is to function as efficiently as possible for the church which it represents in Canada.

First I would like to say a few words as to the present standing of the fishing industry. In 1953 Canadian commercial fishermen landed about 1.8 billion pounds of fish and shellfish, valued at $91 million. In the succeeding ten years landings showed an upward trend which, however, was not consistent from year to year. The annual variations within the trend were largely accounted for by the output of the British Columbia herring fishery and the Newfoundland cod fishery. Despite the rather uneven course of annual landings over this period there was a discernible growth in the value of such landings-that is, in the gross returns to fishermen-and by 1962 this had reached almost $130 million, an increase of $41 million in a period of approximately ten years, or an increase of 43 per cent, most of which was recorded in the last three years.
This satisfying expansion in gross returns to fishermen in the last few years is based,

however, upon a general increase in the prices of the important species, which in turn has resulted from the growing demand for fishery products, principally in Canada and the United States. As we all know, about 80 per cent of the production of Canadian fish processing plants is consumed on this continent, so there is no doubt of the importance of North American consumers to the Canadian fishing industry. The value of exports to the United States in 1962 was $114 million, which is about half of the plant or commercial value of the fishery products of this country. The size of the North American market for fishery products is often described by reference to estimates of per capita consumption of 13 J pounds per person in Canada and about 11 pounds in the United States at the present time. As I have mentioned in this house in previous years, I do not think we should be satisfied with such a limited consumption of fish per capita in a country where the fishing industry is of major importance. We all know that these averages have been quite stable for several years, and this stability is sometimes cited in support of the pessimistic views about consumer acceptance of fishery products on this continent.
With the north American population growing at an annual rate of about 3.5 million, however, the per capita figures obscure an absolute growth in fish consumption of 40 million to 45 million pounds of products each year. This increase in the demand for fishery products requires, on the basis of rough estimation, an additional 80 million to 90 million pounds of raw material. These estimates indicate the magnitude of the additional supply of fish and shellfish required by north American consumers each year and the need for an increased production. The strength or weakness of the continental market has an obvious implication for the Canadian fishing industry. Thus far 1963 has followed the pattern of recent years. Landings for the first eight months are estimated to be 77 million pounds larger than in the same period of 1962. The landed value, however, is about $4.5 million less. On the surface this would seem to contradict what I said earlier about the course of prices. However, the drop in value is attributable principally to the restriction of the salmon catch in British Columbia during the industrial dispute which took place a few months ago. The value of British Columbia salmon landings alone, up to August this year, was $6.6 million less than it was in the first eight months of 1962. This is also reflected in the size of the total pack, which is 1.2 million cases this year as compared with 1.8 million cases last year. This gives only a partial picture of the effect this strike had, not only on

the value of fish production in British Columbia but also on the total economy of that province, which it is estimated has lost well over $10 million. In the Atlantic provinces landings for the first eight months of this year were 48 million pounds larger than in the same period of 1962, and the landed value increased by $3.6 million. These figures represent a continuation of the trend referred to earlier, and which is at least part of the reason for the investment activity which has been pronounced in the region over the last 18 months. Several new plants have been built in Quebec, New Brunswick and Newfoundland, and others are under construction in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. Nineteen large trawlers, over 100 feet in length, have been added to the ground fish fleet, and 11 large draggers to the scallop fleet in the same period.
The demand for fishery products has not only led to higher prices for the additional traditional Atlantic species, but also to efforts to capture and market new species such as the porbeagle and tuna. I am sure all hon. members of the house know what a porbeagle is. It is what is commonly called the mackerel shark. This trend may well continue as more and more effort is exerted upon traditional stocks of ground fish not only by the expanded Canadian fleet, but also by those from other countries.
As hon. members all know, the principal commercial fisheries in Canada are found along our extensive sea coasts. Some of the resources, such as lobster on the Atlantic coast, are localized in areas close to our shores. Others, such as cod, roam over wide areas of the Atlantic ocean in the territorial waters of Canada, as well as hundreds of miles out to the edge of the continental shelf. These fisheries on our east coast have been exploited for several centuries by the fishermen of Europe and the United States, as well as by those of Canada.

As I said, similarly on our Pacific coast the fishery resources on which the Canadian fishing industry depends are accessible to foreign fishermen far beyond Canadian territorial waters. Means must be found to provide adequate protection for these resources so as to assure a sustained yield to present and future generations of Canadian fishermen. For this purpose the government has taken steps to establish a 12-mile exclusive fishery zone along the whole of Canada's coast line, and to implement the straight base-line system as the basis from which Canada's territorial sea and the exclusive fisheries zone will be measured.
Because of treaty rights of certain countries and claims to historic fishing rights of others, discussions with the interested countries have been initiated, with the view to determining the nature and extent of the rights and interests which may be affected by the action which Canada is taking.
As the Prime Minister indicated in his statement last June, it is our hope and belief that we will be able to reach agreement with such countries on mutually satisfactory arrangements.
However, as I mentioned above, resources harvested by Canadian fishermen are also exploited by fishermen of other countries or are accessible to them in the high seas many miles beyond the 12-mile fishing zone. It is therefore necessary to reach agreements with the countries concerned for the protection of these resources. In addition to several treaties which we have with the United States on management of fishery resources of common concern, Canada is a party to two multilateral conventions of great importance to the fishing industries on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of Canada.
On the Pacific coast, the north Pacific fisheries convention between Canada, Japan and the United States, which was brought into force in 1953, has come up for revision at the request of the Japanese government. As I have already informed the house, two conferences have been held, one in Washington last June and the other in Tokyo last month. So far it has not been possible to reach full agreement on a revision which could be accepted by the three countries, but as I reported in my statement to the house on October 9, the Tokyo meeting recessed with a feeling of optimism regarding agreement on a mutually satisfactory convention. The government is hopeful that the recessed conference may be held in Ottawa next spring,

and is taking appropriate steps for that purpose. In the meantime, and I want to emphasize this, the present convention remains in force.
On the Atlantic seaboard the problems of conservation of the resources harvested in the high seas adjacent to our waters are being taken care of by the northwest Atlantic fisheries commission, composed of representatives of 13 nations who are parties to this convention. At the last meeting in June of this year of the commission, on the initiative of Canada an amendment of the convention was proposed, which would make possible the establishment of control measures in the enforcement of conservation regulations.
In the great lakes the lamprey control program of the great lakes fishery commission continues to show encouraging results. In lake Superior over 80 per cent control has been obtained and there are signs of recovery in the important lake trout population. Extension of the control program in lake Michigan and lake Huron is to be continued. Progress made by the commission since its establishment in 1955 is to be reviewed by the contracting parties this year, to determine the desirability of continuing, modifying or terminating the convention, and we are hopeful that the results so far will mean we will carry on with the work which to date has proven so successful.
I wish to speak for a few moments on the modernization, mechanization and expansion of the fishing industry. Many fishing nations are making tremendous progress not only to increase the fishing efficiency of their respective fleets and to expand their fishing operations, but to improve the working conditions of their fishermen, ensure their safety at sea and also improve their earnings.
Just as other industries are moving into the age of electronics and automation, so is the fishing industry. Today even small boats are installing electronic equipment, while the larger deep sea fishing vessels are becoming complex units with electronic navigation, fish-finding and communication equipment, as well as remote control systems and automatic pilots. This in turn means that the need for vocational training within the industry is assuming a position of critical importance.
Recently we have seen where the department's activities in co-operation with the provinces have resulted in the introduction of synthetic fishing gear on the Atlantic coast. Thousands of fishermen who have been engaged in traditional fishing methods are changing to a new type of fishing operation which is resulting in an increase in their per capita landings.

Studies are now being conducted aimed at providing fishermen with an improved design of inshore boat featuring maximum safety, and which will enable a more effective prosecution of the inshore fishery. The department is encouraging the development of a commercial tuna fishery on the east and west coasts, which it is hoped will ultimately lead to the establishment of a permanent tuna fishery in Canada.
The technical services of the department are being made available to the provincial fisheries administrations and to the fishing industry in an increasing extent. Any provincial or industrial enterprise encountering problems in any phase of the fishing industry is invited to seek technical advice from the department.
In addressing the annual meeting of the Fisheries Council of Canada on April 24 last, a few days after resuming the office of Minister of Fisheries, I announced that I proposed to call a federal provincial conference on fisheries development. I then wrote to the ministers responsible for fisheries matters in all ten provinces inviting them to participate in such a conference. I asked the ministers to submit any suggestions they might have for agenda items to be considered at such a conference. I received a most enthusiastic response from all provinces and a long list of very useful suggestions. Earlier this week we had the visit of the minister of fisheries for New Brunswick and his deputy minister. This morning we had with us the minister of industry for the province of Prince Edward Island and his director of fisheries, and both have presented their views and suggestions for this conference.
On this basis, arrangements have been made for the conference, which is now scheduled to take place in Ottawa during the week of January 20, 1964. At this conference all aspects of federal and provincial fisheries administration having a bearing on development of the industry will be discussed. It will be our objective to work out with the provinces the best possible approach to provide those services which are necessary to encourage expansion and development of the industry. It will be our endeavour to overcome impediments to development wherever or whatever they may be. The Canadian fishing industry has made real progress over the last decade, but I am convinced that with a co-ordinated program and encouragement a great deal more can be done toward fully utilizing the sea and fresh water resources available to us. The business of catching, processing and marketing fish is a responsibility of private enterprise, but governments through research, the discovery,
Supply-Fisheries
testing and demonstration of new techniques, the provision of vocational training as required and in other ways, can play a part in achieving maximum results. In the meantime I have been fortunate in having had the opportunity to discuss those questions personally with most of the provincial ministers concerned. I have no doubt whatever that this first national conference on fisheries will prove extremely useful to all concerned and that the national development program which will follow will result in an unprecedented expansion for Canadian fisheries.
The estimates for the department's conservation and development service are, of course, mainly designed to cover normal supply, replacement and maintenance of the protection organization and the established programs in fish culture. These programs are essential for the maintenance of our fisheries and must be continued vigorously. I am sure that most hon. members know of the important work that is being carried out in Canada by the fisheries research board. These research activities fall into three main categories, and broadly may be summarized as research in aquatic biology dealing mainly with fish, research in oceanography and limnology, and research in fisheries technology.
Without going into the full operations of the board at this time I should like to point up some of the work that is being carried out. This year a spring survey was conducted of distribution and abundance of Pacific salmon in the open waters. This shows promise of having real value in forecasting supplies of salmon by species and area on the British Columbia coast which would be of great value to fishing operations.
Expansion of fisheries research has been possible during the past few months through the activities of the board's research vessel, the G. B. Reed, in the Pacific ocean. In its first year of operation the vessel explored potential fishing areas for ground fish and crustaceans in the north gulf of Alaska. A continuing study is being carried out of the oceans as a home for fish covering such subjects as seasonal and year to year variability in temperature and salinity, etc., and the board's work in this field is co-ordinated with other government departments and universities through the Canadian committee on oceanography.
Fisheries research presently going on in Atlantic coast waters includes bottom surveys, which are providing useful forecasts of stock concentrations as a guide to fishing places and times. Studies on the processing of inshore cod in the Newfoundland area has

Supply-Fisheries
been concentrated and given new direction. The physiological condition of fresh caught fish is found to have an important effect on the shelf life and taste of the final products. Methods of impounding the cod to avoid seasonal gluts, pasteurization by gamma irradiation, freeze drying, and a freeze-thaw-refreeze sequence are all under study.
New products, such as fish sausage and fish pancakes, have been developed from freshwater species in the technological laboratories of the board, and these processing methods are now available to processors for commercial use. A new method has also been developed for producing protein concentrate, commonly called fish flour, which has resulted in a product acceptable as human food. The raw material employed in the production of this product can be fish that are of little use at present, or materials that are now being discarded.
Only through maintaining the highest quality in fish and shellfish products can sales be increased at both the domestic and export levels. The department, in co-operation with industry itself, provides inspection services for this purpose. I am happy to report that there has been a continued increase in the acceptance by industry of the voluntary inspection of fresh and frozen fishery products under the Canadian government specification board standards. Consumers also appear to be more aware of the assurance of highest quality given by the maple leaf design on these inspected products.
The Canadian scallop industry has grown at a very rapid rate during recent years. In order that this industry may maintain its reputation for high quality, standards for scallop meat were established following consultation with industry. Compulsory inspection of scallops, including the plants in which they are processed, is now in effect. Further inspection measures have been introduced in other fields.
So that a better service can be given to the inspection of fishery products in northern British Columbia, a permanent fish inspection laboratory service has been made available at Prince Rupert. Because of the very high price attained by lobster, there has been over the years a problem of illegal fishing and processing of this species. The intensified efforts of the department's protection officers coupled with the added check by fish inspection officers appears to have greatly curtailed this illegal operation. An education program has been introduced which has had some result, but I am not satisfied that we have gone far enough. It is our intention to introduce a more practical and effective education program which we hope will reach the fishermen concerned and make them aware
that we are introducing such protective measures for their own benefit and that of future generations. The department is continuing its program of consumer education to bring about a greater use of fish and fishery products in Canadian homes and institutions, and other establishments which cater to group feeding.
Thousands of individual copies of fishery consumer publications are distributed annually by the department's home economists who are strategically located across Canada, and the large number that are requested indicate a growing interest in the use of fish in regular menus. That there is much more interest in using fishery products is also reflected in the number of Canadians who have purchased from the queen's printer the department's large consumer publication entitled "The Canadian Fish Cook Book". This book now going into its fourth printing in English and third in French is one of the queen's printers best sellers.
Audio visual aids, such as film strips and slides, are being widely used by the department to interest and educate the consumer about fishery products, and a stepped up program in this field is being contemplated. At the moment the department has over 550 consumer film strips of five different titles in circulation. The excellence of these film strips which have been produced by the national film board for the department is evidenced by the fact that three of them have won awards at the American film festival in competition with others from many other countries.
Another way in which the department continues to interest those responsible for planning menus to use more fishery products is by the attendance of its home economists at hotel, restaurant, home economic and dietetic conventions. Consumer displays are manned by home economists at these events.
The evolution of fishing and processing methods in various fisheries fields has been spurred in a significant manner by the activities of the department in collaboration with other fisheries agencies, and it is planned to speed the reporting of these new findings to the attention of primary producers through publications and by visual means when possible. Coupled with this will be a greater use of instructional and educational material among fishermen both in printed form and through displays at exhibitions and other events frequented by those in the fishing industry.
In order to keep pace with rising construction costs, the upper limit of value for vessels eligible to come under the low cost insurance of the fishermen's indemnity plan has been increased from $10,000 to $12,500. This plan

has been widely accepted by fishermen. Currently 6,634 vessels valued at $22.5 million are covered. Over the ten years of operation, indemnity payments under the vessel plan have exceeded premium revenue by $126,000 or only $12,600 per year despite the low premium rate of only 1 per cent of appraised value.
This has been but a brief look at some aspects of Canada's fisheries and the efforts that are being made to place this great industry on a sound financial footing so that it may make an even greater contribution to the welfare of the thousands of our people who look to it for their livelihood, and to the nutritional well-being of Canadians.
However, in concluding, there is one further aspect to which I should like to refer for a moment and that is the human element-the fishermen who reap the harvests of the oceans and of our lakes. It is with deep sadness each year that we see men going down to the sea never to return as both our coastal waters and the deeper depths take their toll of lives. It is a tribute to the courage and hardihood of our fishing force that their ranks continue to be strong and enduring. This is a sobering thought, but it is one that urges us to continue our efforts in those fields which will lead to development of fishing craft and gear and other vital equipment which will bring greater measures of safety, comfort and remuneration to our fishermen.
I may have spoken at some length but I felt this was an occasion to put before members of the committee some of the work which has been done by my department. We have in the Department of Fisheries a number of devoted civil servants who have the interests of the fishing industry at heart. As the estimates proceed, I will be in a position to answer the questions which will be put to me by hon. members.

Mr. Chairman,
first, I wish to congratulate the minister upon his opening statement. I must say it is an experience one always remembers to have the first opportunity of presenting estimates as a minister of the crown, before the committee of the whole.

We approved them then, and I speak on behalf of the official opposition when I say we approve them now. We have no intention of prolonging the examination of these estimates on this occasion. I might say, though, that the minister is fortunate tonight, because I suspect this is the best set of estimates he will ever have the honour to present.
All this is not to ignore the responsibility and the opportunity of directing the attention of the committee and, perhaps, of the country, to the important problems which face our fishing industry at the present time. As the proceedings go on, one or two other members of this party will be making brief contributions to the discussion. We reserve the right to take full part in any debate which may develop, should the proceedings be drawn out by members of the committee in other parties.
There is another reason why my remarks will be brief. Because this is an election year we are now far advanced in this fiscal year to which these estimates apply, and eight twelfths of them have, in fact, been granted already by means of interim supply votes. Though this does not limit the right to debate them fully, it means we are far advanced in the fiscal year and the estimates for 1964-65 which are, no doubt, now in the course of preparation are really more current than are the ones we are examining at the present time. In addition, these new estimates should be before the committee, I would think, in the early winter months. At that time we will have an opportunity to examine in more detail the indications of any changes in policy which may have resulted from the views of

the new government and they will be judged fairly, we think, but on their merits, be they good or bad.
In passing I want to mention a general subject which the minister has dealt with having to do with the importance of the fishing industry in Canada. The fishing industry in Canada has been remaining fairly constant over the last few years, in common with those of some of the other important fishing countries of the world, but in terms of percentage of the world's fish catch Canada is dropping down. This is partly due to the natural development of some of the highly populated countries of the world. Great strides have been made in those countries in developing means of reaping the resources of the seas as a source of protein food.
But this brings into focus perhaps the most important problem of the industry. The living resources of the sea, unlike almost any other natural resource, are common resources. They are owned in common not only by the people of one country but by those of all countries of the world-in other words, by humanity as a whole. One of the great problems that has to be solved in the future is the finding of a rational and reasonable means of fair exploitation of these resources and the carrying on jointly of reasonable conservation methods by the countries of the world to preserve these common resources to be exploited by all.
In this connection, as the minister pointed out, we are a party to seven different fisheries treaties, I believe. These treaties have to be renegotiated. Conferences are constantly being held in connection with them and this puts a very great load on the departmental officials. The department is in a unique situation in this regard. It is relatively small but it has these great responsibilities. I would recommend most strongly that the government give consideration to setting up in the Department of Fisheries a special branch to deal continuously with our international obligations. It is a matter that has been given brief consideration in the past but the situation is becoming more complicated. I hope this suggestion will not be lost sight of because I believe these great responsibilities place an unreasonable load on the administrative officers of the department who have their regular duties to perform as well as safeguarding Canada's interests in this connection.
This is a very important and complex problem. Some people may believe that we can preserve our interests in this regard simply by extending our territorial waters. This is of some advantage but it does not meet the problem by any means because fish are no respecters of boundaries. Many species migrate over wide areas of the ocean.

Those types of fish which spend their entire life cycle in the high seas are, of course, a truly common resource and there is the problem of sharing them reasonably between ourselves and other countries.
But the situation is much more complicated than that. Some of our most valuable species of fish are, of course, fish that spend part of their lives in our territorial waters and part in our national fresh waters. Certain rivers are reserved to a great extent in a state that will permit the generation of new stocks of the species which then spend most of their lives in the ocean. We have the problem of establishing our proprietary interest in those stocks of fish that exist because of special measures, some of which are quite expensive, which we as a nation have taken. With respect to the north Pacific fisheries treaty, I hope it will be possible for Canada to maintain the abstention principle in this connection.
As I have pointed out, although Canada's fishing industry has remained quite healthy other nations have expanded their fishing industries at a tremendous rate. Over the last 10 years the fishing industry of Japan has grown by about 77 per cent and that of the U.S.S.R. has more than doubled. Therefore we are in a very competitive field and I am pleased that the minister has noted the importance of developing new and more efficient methods of catching, processing and marketing fish.
In this connection he also noted the expansion in the building of new types of fishing vessels on both coasts. This stimulation of the shipbuilding industry is due in part to the subsidization of the industry and I am glad it is bearing fruit as it appears to be. As is generally known, this policy was instituted by the previous government.
This leads me to the point of stating that there are many facilities and services for the fishing industry which are supplied by other departments, but I will not discuss them at the present time except to mention that the Deparment of Public Works, the Department of Transport and the Department of Labour all have an interest in the fishing industry. Taxpayers' money is being spent through these other departments to some extent for the benefit of the fishing industry, so it is not fair to assume that the items appearing under the Department of Fisheries represent the only money that Canada is spending in the interests of the industry.
I mentioned in passing the fact that the extension of our territorial ^waters is of considerable interest to the fishing industry. I believe this will solve certain problems but it will not solve others. In this connection

the government has announced its intention to extend Canada's territorial waters to 12 miles within the year. I hope the minister will take under advisement the importance of strengthening our protective service so that we can properly police the additional areas of water. I know he will have an ardent ally in his colleague, the Secretary of State, when he tries to get additional sums approved by treasury board for this purpose. In this connection I think it is even more important that action be taken to make certain without any doubt that such bodies of water as the gulf of St. Lawrence, the bay of Fundy, Dixon entrance and Hecate strait are established to be Canadian national waters and our property.
There are many other important factors and situations which I should like to discuss for a little while tonight. However, as I said, it is not our intention to prolong the examination of these estimates unnecessarily. So, Mr. Chairman, I will leave any further remarks I might have until a later time when the individual items are called or, if the committee is in a co-operative mood and wishes to pass the estimates rapidly tonight, I would be quite content to leave any further remarks I might have on this important subject until the estimates for the next fiscal year are before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I think the first thing I should do in a public way is extend congratulations to the minister upon his appointment to this cabinet position. I did that by way of correspondence on April 27 in a letter which contained a reference to other things. So far, I have not had a reply from the minister, so perhaps he should check back on his correspondence to see what happened to that letter and deal with the other matters in it.
I was interested in listening to the introductory remarks of the minister. They seemed to be composed mostly of a recitation of statistics and screenings from various departmental publications that had been issued over the years, especially this past year. When it came to an announcement of any definite policy that the fisheries department expected to promote, or what the government hoped to accomplish by its fisheries policy, we found the minister's speech just as barren as many of the fish-hooks of the fishermen when they pull them from the water. The only exception was a reference by the minister to a federal-provincial conference on fisheries matters which, if I understood him correctly, is to be held on January 20 next year. This is welcome news. I wish the Minister of Public Works would act with the same alacrity in promoting a federal-provincial conference on highways, and that the Prime 28902-5-253J

In any event, I hope that out of this conference there does come something concrete, something worth while, something that could point the way for this government in the years ahead in so far as policy matters are concerned.
We in the New Democratic party have had an interest in fisheries for quite some length of time, both at the federal and provincial levels. Over the years we have made many proposals, some of which were ridiculed at the time they were made. Some of them now are in the process of being accepted. The minister referred to one such proposal, namely the breadth of our territorial seas. I am sure many members of this house, if they will look back a few years, will recall when I, on behalf of this party, introduced a bill to extend the territorial sea to 12 miles on a unilateral basis the proposal was ridiculed by members in all parts of the house. Now, the principle seems to be accepted, and this is precisely what we are attempting to do.
I would remind the minister that, in respect of the announcement to extend the territorial sea to 12 miles, there was a specific campaign promise by his party that the territorial sea would include Hecate strait on the west coast. I hope the minister and his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs remember this promise when it comes time to actually make the pronouncement. I do not think we should look upon the 12 mile limit, as it is referred to, as the solution for all problems confronting the fishing industry in Canada. Certainly, it is not. It is a solution for some species of fish, bottom fish and the like, but not for all of them. We should never lose sight of this fact.
So far as we are concerned, I think we could enunciate some of the objectives, some of the goals which the department and the minister should have in mind. These should be clearly established as the guideposts for what we do in fisheries matters in the years ahead. The first one is to look upon fisheries resources as we do upon all renewable resources, from the point of view of conservation to ensure that future generations will have the opportunity to exploit this natural resource just as we do today. Second, we should promote the extensive exploitation of these resources within the bounds established by the conservation principle. In doing this, we should take cognizance of the fact that there is this tremendous population explosion, as it has been called. This increase in population automatically creates increased pressure

to find additional sources of food. This increased demand for food is automatically pressuring nations into searching the sea for the additional food that is required.
Recently the United Nations released some figures in respect of this, and perhaps I could refer to them very briefly. In the period from 1948 to 1960 the increase in the supply of meat was 19 per cent. During that same period, the increase in the world supply of fish, as distinct from meat, was close to 50 per cent. This indicates the tremendous increase in the world supply of fish within a 12-year period. It also indicates the tremendous increase in the catch and in the interest of other nations.
As the minister has just indicated, other countries are developing bigger fishing fleets, bigger boats, floating canneries, and so on. All of these things create increased pressure upon the fisheries resources that are available throughout the world. Different species of fish are influenced in different ways by this. Some of our species, for instance salmon and herring, migrate out to sea, while others stay close to the shore where we are able to protect them. Our salmon and herring, being migratory, are vulnerable to the increased activity and pressure on our fisheries by other nations. Perhaps one nation concerned is a nation involved in the north Pacific fisheries commission to which the minister referred.
I think what we must do, having in mind this increased pressure on the fisheries of the world, is to bend our efforts towards a concentration of activity on international agreements to ensure that the conservation measures we engage in at home are not destroyed by wanton fishing on the high seas by other nations, to ensure that throughout the world there is some sense of reasonableness in the exploitation of our fisheries. I should like to make some comments on the north Pacific fisheries treaty itself, and, specifically on the recommendation which the commission made about a year ago to the effect that Japan should be permitted to fish for herring off the west coast of the Queen Charlotte islands and the eastern Bering sea.
I think it is very regrettable that after all the discussion and the interest that brewed up over this particular question the Liberal party, by a sleight of hand process, agreed to those recommendations in the manner in which they did. The impression was at least left, if it was not specifically stated, that this subject matter and this question would be referred to the marine and fisheries committee so that a thorough investigation could be made into it before the recommendations were dealt with one way or the other. But on the eve of parliament meeting-about a week before-by a secret method, and not by an

open, declared order in council, this government put into effect the recommendations of the commission of last fall and announced them by telephone, not by way of any formal communication. It is unfortunate that at the very moment the minister was in Vancouver meeting and discussing with delegations from the various sections of the fishing industry this vitally important question, in the back of his mind he was preparing the way to proceed in order to recommend the acceptance of these recommendations. We would like to have in these matters some above-the-table dealings, some confidence in the government in this regard, so that the people of this nation and especially this parliament know just what is taking place. Specifically we would like to know about the north Pacific fisheries negotiations and what steps are being taken to deal with other nations of the world in agreements relating to the fisheries of the world.
One of the specific campaign promises of the Liberal party

another one-was that the Soviet union would definitely be brought into the north Pacific treaty. We know that the Soviet union contributes to the fishery stocks of the north Pacific; we know that she has a high seas fishing fleet; we know that she ranges a long way over to this side of the Pacific ocean in her fisheries and research work. There is nothing whatever to stop the Soviet union cruising in to within three miles of our shore, as it is now, or 12 miles when the 12 mile limit is established-it does not really matter which it is-and lying in wait for salmon which are waiting in our waters to come home to spawn, scooping them up and leaving nothing for future generations. The only thing that deters Japan, for instance, engaging in this sort of activity is, as the minister stated, the north Pacific fisheries treaty. The Liberal party realized this during an election campaign period, made a specific promise about it, and so far we have not heard a single, solitary word about what steps this government is taking to put into effect what was a reasonable, legitimate and sensible campaign promise.
We inquired of the minister about it earlier this session. His answer at that time was generally to the effect that maybe this matter was being discussed in Washington, and perhaps he should not say any more about it until those meetings were concluded. We would like to know, the people of Canada would like to know, and I am sure the people of the world would like to know what is taking place with respect to getting the Soviet union into the north Pacific fisheries treaty; because if we do not, you can bet your bottom dollar that the Soviet union, because of the pressure from people demanding food in that

country, will be looking for further sources of food supply from the sea and will automatically look for salmon which is not of their own origination, in order that their salmon can come back home again and spawn for the years to come.
I do not understand why the Soviet union will perhaps not enter into an agreement such as the north Pacific fisheries treaty, if they were approached on this subject and asked about it as long ago as 1957 or 1958. I am given to understand that Japan and the Soviet union have had a convention relating to the salmon fisheries of the Asian area, and there is no reason why the Soviet union would not be interested in engaging in a similar sort of treaty in which we and the United States were involved. We would like to have a very clear indication from the minister as to whether the campaign promises which his party made in the election campaign really mean anything now. We ask him what he is doing, has been doing or intends to do about seeing them put into effect.
A vitally important field, I think, is leading or getting this government to point itself in the direction of international agreements and high seas conservation measures, to ensure that future generations have fish for their children as we desire to have this food for ours. When it comes to matters that concern us more directly in a national or domestic way, I think we all realize that the east and west coast fisheries differ; that there are different species of fish on these coasts; that there are different methods of catching them, and there are different economics, and so on, involved as between the east and west coasts. Since 1957 we have had, at least from the practicalities of administration point of view, an orientation toward the east coast. The hon. member from Queens, when he was a member of the Conservative cabinet, was the minister of fisheries. He is, of course, from the east coast, as is the present Minister of Fisheries. Without casting any reflection upon the ideas or attitudes of ministers, it is an automatic fact of politics that one's hometown induces the greatest pressure to do things, as distinct from communities which are further away.
If we look at this year's estimates, for instance, just as one example, without going into the details in a way contrary to the rules, we see that vote 155, which involves a very important field, namely educational work in fisheries techniques and co-operative producing and selling among fishermen, concerns a total amount of $120,000, with the east coast fisheries receiving ten times that of the west coast. I am not saying they should not, because this is a vitally important contribution; but it does show that there is

heavier emphasis, even in that one vote, given to the east coast than there is to the west. I am not saying this is wrong in so far as the east coast is concerned.
We find that the Fisheries Prices Support Act has its greatest, if not exclusive, application to east coast fishermen and is practically unused on the west coast. The Newfoundland bait service is, again, directly connected to the east coast fisheries, and salt fish assistance and the like. Perhaps the only act under which the west coast fisheries might have some advantage is the Cold Storage Act, which allows for subsidies to be given for the building of cold storages. Unfortunately this is not under the Department of Fisheries; it is in the hands of the Minister of Agriculture, which is an extremely sad state of affairs not only for fishermen but for agriculturists as well. In addition to that, subsidies under this act have been suspended, so what advantage fishermen on the west coast might have had in receiving cold storage subsidies has gone, because there is no more to be obtained under that act.
On the order paper there is a resolution to appoint two ministers of agriculture, one for the east and one for the west. I understand that one of the ministers has already appointed himself to this particular position and is merely waiting for the formality of the measure going through parliament, if it gets that far. But if it is sensible or reasonable, and this government thinks it is a correct thing, to have a minister of agriculture for the east and one for the west, it is even more important to have two ministers of fisheries, one for the east and one for the west, so that west coast fisheries can receive the fullest possible consideration from the federal government.
We would like to make some specific suggestions to the minister and his department. These suggestions are at this stage along rather broad lines, because they involve what we consider to be questions of policy connected with the principles we enunciated earlier, namely those of conservation, exploitation and a recognition of the growing population of the world and the importance of fishery products as a source of protein.
We think that the research attitudes in the Department of Fisheries should find their way into the levels of discussion on policy. In this regard, without any reflection upon the individuals concerned, we find that the present deputy minister, Dr. Needier, a scientist in the field of fisheries, is likely to bring into the policy level of the department the attitude, concept and ideas of a research scientist.

This contrasts somewhat with the attitude which existed previously when the late Mr. Clark was the deputy minister.
This is no reflection whatsoever upon Mr. Clark. He was a very able, competent, personable gentleman in this field and he administered the department very effectively; but Mr. Clark was a practical man from the industrial side of fisheries. He was an administrator, not a scientist; and now we hope that the attitudes, opinions and research ideas of the people in the department will have some bearing on what is decided upon from a policy point of view, because research is essential to develop not only the fisheries of Canada but those of other countries.
We may have to pump extensive amounts of money into the research side of the department's activities. We should no longer look upon the fisheries research board-a wonderful organization

as being just an organization that exists and carries on from day to day. We think it should be more adequately financed, and that more direction and freedom should be given it in order to find ways and methods of increasing the catch, processing, and consumption of fishery products. If I may in passing, I would like to make reference to Dr. Kask, who left the chairmanship of the fisheries research board early this year. I am sure the minister and his predecessors in the department found Dr. Kask and his associates invaluable in the work which they did.
There is an interesting sidelight to the activities of the fisheries research board, and that is that throughout the year it produces a number of publications and documents based upon the research studies which it conducts. It is interesting to realize just who reads these publications and documents the most aptly, and who accepts them as guideposts in fishing. It is a well known fact that fishing skippers and captains of the Soviet union fishing fleet look upon the research department's publications as their bible in exploiting our fisheries on the high seas. It is unfortunate that our own fisheries people do not do the same thing, and that our fishing industry does not follow the activities of the board with such fervour.
The minister mentioned the development of fish flour for human consumption. I think much greater activity must be devoted to this field, to process fishery products which are not presently edible because they are not exotic enough, and to process what is now more or less considered to be waste from fish plants. These should be processed into protein concentrates for human consumption. The board should also be concerning itself with the possibility of the plant life of the oceans being processed for human consumption, because it is also a source of food.

We should look ahead to the time when the world's production and consumption of fish will be perhaps two or three times what it is now, ranging upwards of 100 million tons a year, something which we could not conceive of some ten or 12 years ago. The policy of the department and the government must be directed towards preparing for this, through early planning of our investment in fisheries, in catching fish, processing them and distributing them to the point where we will remain a prominent power in world fisheries in years to come. We are that at present, but we will not be in the future if we keep fumbling along on a day to day or year to year basis.
We should also be promoting extensive use of artificial or man made hatcheries for fish because, even though we may not like it, I think in time to come we will see a greater multiple use of lakes, rivers and waters, and we will find that pesticides, insecticides, sewage and pollution coming from industries, cities and towns will increase as time goes on and will take their toll of the natural spawning grounds in lakes and other waters.
In this regard I was very pleased to note that the minister, the deputy minister and a couple of other officials-Dr. Pritchard for one comes to mind-appeared before the committee on food and drugs just the other day, and dealt with the question of the effect of insecticides and pesticides on marine life and fisheries. Unfortunately I do not think that committee, because of the complexity of the subject before it, will be able to come up with any scientific, technical and worth-while recommendations in this particular field.
If I may digress for a moment, this is one committee, perhaps more than any other standing or special committee of the house, that should have an extensive research staff provided for it, so that it can deal with the various bits of scientific and technical information presented to it, analyse that information and then, when it makes recommendations, it will know what it is doing. Without that, a great deal of the activity of the committee will be a waste of time.
As I said earlier, we must get into the field of expansion in our relations with other countries concerning international fishery conventions. We must also think in terms of the promotion of fishery colleges and enticement of more people into scientific research in those fields which relate to the ocean and to the plant and animal life therein. If we do these things, if the minister keeps them in mind from a long range and short range policy point of view, and if he takes steps to implement them, we will continue to be one of the leading fishery nations of the world.

In closing I would like to make one comment in the nature of a commendation. As I know them, and as they are known by people in the fishing industry, the officials, scientists and officers on the staff of the Department of Fisheries are respected and admired. They are doing a tremendous job. We would like to see them get on with it, and be provided with the money and policy directions that will enable them to continue to do a remarkable job.

Mr. Chairman, following the example of those who have preceded me in this debate, I intend to be relatively brief in my remarks. This is not because the Department of Fisheries or the fishery industry is of small concern or of little value to our nation. The contrary is true; but unfortunately I am afraid many people across the country are not aware of the true value of the industry, not only to the hundreds who are directly involved in it but also to the provinces in which fish resources are found, and to the national economy.
The suggestion has been made by the hon. member for Skeena that it might be advisable to have two ministers of fisheries, one for the east and one for the west, and to bolster his argument he referred to the proposal to have two ministers of agriculture. Personally I am not convinced that it is wise policy in either department, because once we set the precedent we may find that we end up with two cabinets, with ministers of this and that, and another group for east and west, until instead of having about 20 ministers, as we have now, we have 40. I do not think this would be too good for the country. Possibly we are in too great a danger of fragmentation as it is. I have always taken the position that as far as national policy is concerned it should be a national policy, and if any adaptations are necessary with regard to specific areas they can be worked out. I believe policy should be evolved which will apply as far as possible right across the nation. I do not think it is necessary to have two ministers if the minister would just become aware that Canada is Canada from coast to coast and that his sights do not just rest on the one side but also are set on the other. I am inclined to think the minister could improve his position substantially if a little closer attention were given to problems on the west coast and to the representation of the fishermen on the west coast.

I pointed out at that time that we are not too concerned perhaps with the way it is expressed, but we are certainly concerned that the abstention principle should be incorporated in the treaty in the course of these renegotiations.
Also with regard to conservation I should like to refer to the closure regulations as they affect the Fraser river and other areas of British Columbia. The minister is aware that just at the time he was leaving for Tokyo a meeting was held by the fishermen in

Steveston. There were several hundred fishermen gathered there to make representations in connection with the north Pacific treaty, and they also met in a special way to deal with the closures imposed on the Fraser river, which was one of the main concerns at that time. There was a feeling that the method by which the closures were implemented was most unfair. Let me say again that they were not opposing the principle of conservation. They recognize that it is essential to the welfare of the whole industry. But the fishermen of the Fraser river, especially, felt they were being discriminated against because, for
them,	they faced what amounted to a total closure of the river. It is true it was opened up one day a week but I think there were some weeks when no fishing at all was allowed. Meanwhile, those who fished off the coast enjoyed almost unlimited freedom; they were allowed to fish several days a week.
The fishermen of the Fraser valley had a legitimate complaint. They were almost completely barred from engaging in fishing in their own areas. They were not equipped to fish off the coast; their boats and gear would not permit them to go so far. So here were men who depended on fishing for a living, yet could not take advantage of the fishing in the Fraser river basin for themselves and their families. A serious endeavour should be made to see that fishermen in every area have an opportunity to share in the resources to the conservation of which they have contributed. It may be that the conference which is to be held will lead to the solution of some of these problems. Perhaps it will lead to better relations between the fishermen, the industry in general and the government at various levels. As I say, I believe this is one of the important resources of the nation and one which makes a substantial contribution to the economic welfare, not only of those directly concerned but of Canada from coast to coast.

Mr. Chairman, I feel bound to express in this house the views of the inshore fishermen of the Gaspe peninsula and to deal with two matters pertaining to fisheries. First of all, the establishment of fishing limits for trawlers, as well as international limits, and
then,	the report of the committee of inquiry on the Unemployment Insurance Act, and the recommendations of the same committee with regard to fisheries.
Mr. Chairman, in the last few years, the inshore fishermen of the gulf of St. Lawrence and of part of the Baie des Chaleurs have been at war with trawlers which, apart from plundering the inshore fishing territories usually reserved to fishermen who go in for fishing on a small scale, damage fishing

tackle and are guilty of offences that are termed as acts of piracy in some places.
Mr. Chairman, most commercial fishermen of the Gaspe peninsula, namely about 85 per cent, are inshore fishermen who operate in a strip, a few miles wide, along the coast of the Gaspe peninsula. Their fishing trips last only a day; they start very early in the morning and come back around noon. In addition, their fishing season lasts only six months a year, and it is also necessary to take into account the days lost as a result of bad weather.
The main species of fish taken is the ground fish, among which cod is the most common. And there seems to exist in my constituency a long term trend towards decrease in the fishing volume and in the number of fishermen.
But this year, at least at the beginning of the season, the number of small fishermen increased in the Gaspe peninsula, because of a certain stagnation in the field of employment.
Unfortunately, so far, the quantities of landed cod have been 20 per cent smaller than last year, a factor which certainly will not encourage newcomers to become full time fishermen.
Even if we take into account the natural fluctuations which cause the catches to vary, we still have to admit that in that area the fish stock diminishes, and that the size of the fish seems to be shrinking.
We are confronted with unmistakable signs of over-exploitation of stocks, and the culprits are not exclusively the 60 to 65 feet long trawlers which operate along the Quebec coast, or in the maritime provinces, and more particularly in New Brunswick.
It seems that foreign boats operating inside the gulf of St. Lawrence have a direct influence. Figures have been mentioned in respect to the catch of those foreign boats, and they were about 100 million pounds per year. It is impossible to get more details on that matter, indeed it is rather difficult to compile accurate data, since those boats from various countries do not submit reports on their activities.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, in the gulf of St. Lawrence only, foreign boats took over 100 million pounds of cod, according to a report published by the d.b.s. Now, in 1962, the cod catch in eastern Canada, including Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, amounted to 585,643,000 pounds. And in the Gaspe area only, in the gulf of St. Lawrence, foreign boats have caught a hundred million pounds of cod a year.

In view of this situation, I am of the opinion that it is urgent that the 12-mile limit be put into effect; this should close completely the gulf of St. Lawrence to foreign boats.
Moreover, we must consider that the fish population of the gulf of St. Lawrence is the same as in the northwest Atlantic, on the banks of Newfoundland, on the banks of Nova Scotia and on the north coast as far as Greenland.
Let us come back to the gulf of St. Lawrence and the Chaleur bay, where stocks of fish have been replenished. Coastal fishing should be extended to other areas, and I wish to mention now as an example the island of Anticosti for the fishermen of the north coast of the Gaspe peninsula. If coastal fishing was thus extended, more intensive research should be done in order to vary fishing techniques and design suitable boats, such as trawlers.
We should aim for diversified ways of catching fish and try to add new techniques to the existing ones. It would be necessary also to step up research to find out the extent of our resources; there are ways to catch other kinds of fish besides ground fish like cod. In the area of Anticosti island-I will use it again as an example; it is a high point because of the possibilities it offers- there are banks of shrimp, lobster, scallops, crab and other fish like halibut, which have another commercial value and are far from being used in full.
To round up the research work that needs to be done, it would also be advisable to have the research board draw up fishing maps giving indications on the nature of the fish banks, on the movement of water caused by tides or currents, which would determine the fishing conditions in the area.
Mr. Chairman, I am coming to the reason for those explanations. Those maps will have to show also the areas reserved for inshore fishing.
I understand the situation with regard to the federal jurisdiction on fisheries, and that of Quebec as well as of New Brunswick as regards those interprovincial limits is somewhat confused, but the Minister of Fisheries said last summer, in the Magdalen islands, that an investigation is being carried out with the help of experts from Ottawa, Quebec and Fredericton, and personally, I hope that a settlement will be reached in the spring of 1964 so that a strip of a few miles may be reserved for inshore fishermen or private fishing on a small scale.
I even suggest-I admit that would be something new-that a license or permit costing $1 or $2 be required from fishermen so that they might enjoy some privileges and be obliged to follow some regulations.

The road map that the fisherman will receive with his licence would serve as a guide to him. In my opinion, that coastguard squad should be increased and should see that the regulations are enforced in those fishing areas reserved for small fishermen. The fisherman who would violate the regulations might lose his permit for a period set by the law.
Finally, it seems important to recommend assistance plans for the construction of fishing boats now in effect. That assistance should be extended in order to include fishing boats 35 feet long instead of 45 feet.
That sector of coastal fishing will grow more important and will certainly be selfsupporting, because on the basis I have already mentioned, with a somewhat larger territory, with a wider variety of fishing techniques, fishermen will be able to depend on various kinds of fish instead of limiting themselves to cod.
In that way, the fishermen could secure a much higher income and depend for their livelihood on fishing alone, without resorting to social welfare benefits.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Chairman, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries, a question which is inspired by the numerous requests of the fishermen of my constituency.
Those people feel that unemployment insurance benefits coming to them next winter will be nothing but peanuts, because the landings of fish have been 20 per cent smaller than the previous year. One can only too easily understand their worries. Actually, I know families with eight, nine or ten children, who will collect no more than $20 a week, because their contributions have been smaller than last year.
We have to admit that the fishing industry is riddled with serious problems. Quite a number of fishermen suffer from chronic unemployment, and are incapable of maintaining, without outside help, a decent standard of living.
In the report of the inquiry commission on the Unemployment Insurance Act, the commissioners recommended the following:
That a separate plan be established for the benefit of Independent fishermen and that such a plan be more consistent with their situation and their requirements than the general unemployment insurance plan could be, and that the Department of Fisheries be vested with the responsibility of administering that plan.
In conclusion, I wish to put a question to the Minister of Fisheries. Did the officials of the Department of Labour ever meet with those of the Department of Fisheries in connection with that recommendation of the commissioners?

Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the statement made by the Minister of Fisheries and as the representative of Queens-Lunenburg, a riding in which is located the largest deep sea fishing fleet in North America, I wish to comment briefly on some of the problems relating to the fishing industry. I should first like to congratulate the minister on his appointment to his portfolio. I know that his experience in the house and his prior experience in the fishing industry will serve him well in carrying out his present responsibilities. I also know that as a maritimer he will give careful consideration to all problems pertaining to the fishing industry and especially those pertaining to the Atlantic provinces.
Canada is today the seventh largest fishing nation in the world and the fifth largest trading nation, possessing the world's longest coast line. A few years ago we knew very little about our continental shelf, but as the world's population continues to grow we shall have to look to the sea for increasingly larger amounts of edible protein.
At the present time the fishing industry is in some ways at the stage at which primitive man was many centuries ago. We hunt the fish that nature provides, just as our ancestors hunted animals for food. We have not yet begun to herd fish or improve their quality, but I believe that one day in the not too distant future we shall be forced to farm the sea as we do the land. In order to do this we shall have to give increased emphasis to our oceanographic research. We shall have to study the organic matter dissolved in sea water which activates the whole growth process. After all, on land the strain of cattle has been improved by careful breeding and at the same time the productivity of the soil has been increased by weeding and by fertilizing. It is almost certain that a similar approach to the sea will enable us to harvest a much larger crop of fish, instead of worrying as we do now about protecting our fishing rights from the depredations of fleets from other nations.
We should be able to produce plenty of edible seafood for everybody, if we discover and apply good methods of sea husbandry. A start has already been made along these lines. It was made by the previous administration under the leadership of the former prime minister. An oceanographic institute, the first of its kind in Canada, was opened last year at Bedford basin near Halifax. While this institute was opened under the auspices of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, still it has a branch for the fisheries department. As a result our

marine laboratories are expanding. Graduate students are being trained in all aspects of oceanography. New research ships are carrying out scientific investigations along our coasts. We can, therefore, expect rapid development in the next few years. We are not alone in this work, for all major maritime nations are now taking part. Throughout the world roughly 50 research ships are constantly at sea carrying approximately 600 technicians and trained people.
Through this increase in scientific effort we hope to plug a big gap in our knowledge concerning the earth on which we live, and we hope to learn more about the habits of the fish, which are part of the food resources which automatically renew themselves. In its natural state, acre for acre, the sea is producing as much as the land; yet man is only taking about 1 per cent of his present food requirements from the ocean. When we come to farm the ocean we can expect it to produce a much greater quantity of desirable food, just as scientific farming on the land has improved the production of grain and vegetables. Through the proper management of the ocean, we can greatly increase our well-being on the land, but this will have to be done by international agreement. Some countries have already made a start along these lines. Japan is trying out salt pond farms in the inland sea, where yellowtail are raised and dumped into the adjacent sea when grown. England is farming plaice somewhat in the same manner as trout rivers are restocked, and we are raising oysters in Prince Edward Island to help re-establish that industry. I must give due credit for this to the officials of the department, some of whom are present with us tonight.
In my opinion, research along these lines should be expanded. We are not doing enough to restock our rivers and our lakes with trout and with salmon, especially in the Atlantic region and in my own province of Nova Scotia. If further developments were carried out along these lines, these fish would not only provide a valuable source of food but they would also encourage tourists to visit Canada in greater numbers, thereby bringing greater economic benefits to everyone. I would, therefore, urge upon the minister to give consideration to the scientific development of our fisheries when he sits down to review plans for next year's estimates.
I know this government and the present minister are greatly concerned over conservation. I listened with interest on June 4 when the Prime Minister made a statement to the house on the law of the sea and his plans to unilaterally establish a 12-mile exclusive fisheries zone along the whole of the

Canadian coastline somewhere about midMay, 1964. This action, of course, will be beneficial to our inshore fishermen, but it will not materially affect the landings of our deep sea fleet. It will create problems with France and the United States, both of whom have treaty rights in some of the areas affected. It will also create problems with Portugal, a country which has a traditional fishing right on our coast. It is regrettable that this action had to be taken unilaterally.
